parole.significato: killing

parole.significato: killer

parole.significato: used to form adjectives, of or befitting -cracy

parole.significato: Used to form an occupational noun denoting someone associated with, concerned with, or engaged in a specified activity.

parole.significato: Forming the names of dynasts, being suffixed to the name of their progenitors and meaning “descendant of”.

parole.significato: Forming names of feminine equivalents or of feminine descendants from a masculine name.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French -ide f, from Latin -is f (genitive: -idis; plural: -ides), from Ancient Greek -ῐς f (-ĭs) (genitive: -ῐδος (-ĭdos); plural: -ῐδες (-ĭdes)).

parole.significato: An action or process, or the result of an action or process.
parole.testo: Reanalysed from -ation, -tion, from Middle French -tion, -cion, from Latin -tiō. By surface analysis, this suffix is added to verbs derived from Latin perfect participle stems.

parole.significato: Used to forms nouns of state, condition or quality.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French -itude, from Latin -(i)tūdō. By surface analysis, -i- + -tude.

parole.significato: Indicative of a pause or discontinuance.
parole.testo: From Middle French pause, from Latin pausa, from Ancient Greek παῦσις (paûsis, “discontinuance”).

parole.significato: Towards; Used to indicate direction, reduction to, increase to, change into, or motion.
parole.testo: Assimilated form of ad- before b, sc, sp, st, and sometimes m. From Middle English a-, from Middle French a-, from Latin ad (“towards”).

parole.significato: The fat surrounding the belly.
parole.testo: First attested in 1541 as labdomen. Borrowed from Middle French abdomen as well as from its etymon Latin abdōmen, possibly from abdō (“conceal”), from ab (“away”) + -dō (“put, place”).

parole.significato: To regard (someone or something) as horrifying or detestable; to feel great repugnance toward.

parole.significato: To end a law, system, institution, custom or practice.
parole.testo: From late Middle English abolisshen, from Middle French aboliss-, extended stem of abolir, from Latin abolēre (“to retard, check the growth of, (and by extension) destroy, abolish”), and inchoative abolēscere (“to wither, vanish, cease”).

parole.significato: The act of abolishing; an annulling; abrogation.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French abolition, from Old French abolucion, a learned borrowing from Latin abolitiōnem. First attested in 1529. Equivalent to abolish + -tion.

parole.significato: The act of abrogating.
parole.testo: First attested in 1535. From Middle French abrogation, from Latin abrogātiō (“repealed”), from abrogo, from ab (“from”) + rogo (“ask, inquire”). By surface analysis, ab- + Latin rog- + -ate + -ion.

parole.significato: Being away from a place; withdrawn from a place; existing but not present; (sometimes) missing.
parole.testo: From Middle English absent, from Middle French absent, from Old French ausent, and their source, Latin absens, present participle of absum (“to be away from”), from ab (“away”) + sum (“to be”).

parole.significato: The herb absinthium Artemisia absinthium (grande wormwood); essence of wormwood.

parole.testo: First attested around 1380. parole.significato: To include so that it no longer has separate existence; to overwhelm; to cause to disappear as if by swallowing up; to…

parole.significato: Cleansing; purging; abstergent.
parole.testo: From Middle French abstersif, from Latin abstersus.

parole.significato: Contrary to reason or propriety; obviously and flatly opposed to manifest truth; inconsistent with the plain dictates o…
parole.testo: First attested in 1557. From Middle French absurde, from Latin absurdus (“incongruous, dissonant, out of tune”), from ab (“away from, out”) + surdus (“silent, deaf, dull-sounding”). Compare surd.

parole.significato: To put to a wrong use; to misapply; to use improperly; to use for a wrong purpose or end; to pervert
parole.testo: From Middle English abusen, from Middle French abuser, from Latin abūsus (“misused, using up”), perfect active participle of abūtor (“to use up, misuse, consume”), from ab (“from, away from”) + ūtor (“to use”).

parole.significato: To express the accent of vocally; to utter with accent.
parole.testo: From Middle French accenter, from Old French accenter, from Latin accentō, from accentus.

parole.significato: Acceptation; received meaning.
parole.testo: From Middle English accepcioun, from Middle French accepcion (Modern French acception) and Latin acceptiō, acceptiōnis (“acceptance”). By surface analysis, accept + -ion.

parole.significato: The act of amassing or gathering, as into a pile.
parole.testo: From Middle English acumulacyon, from Middle French accumulation and its etymon, Latin accumulātiō, accumulātiōnis. By surface analysis, accumulate + -ion. First attested in the late 15th century. Doublet of accumulatio.

parole.significato: Pertaining to, or containing, an accusation.
parole.testo: From Middle English accusatorie, from Middle French accusatorie and its etymon Latin accūsātōrius. By surface analysis, accuse + -atory.

parole.significato: To rest satisfied, or apparently satisfied, or to rest without opposition and discontent (usually implying previous opp…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French acquiescer, from Latin acquiescō; ad + quiescō (“to rest”), from quies (“rest”).

parole.significato: A sharp and bitter hatred.
parole.testo: From Middle French acrimonie, from Latin ācrimōnia (“sharpness, pungency”).

parole.significato: The state or quality of being active; activeness.
parole.testo: From Middle French activité, from Latin activitas. Equivalent to active + -ity.

parole.significato: An old saying which has obtained credit by long use.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French adage, from Latin adā̆gium.

parole.significato: The upper arm, as opposed to the forearm.

parole.significato: Deserving of the highest esteem or admiration; estimable.
parole.testo: From Middle English admyrable, partly from Middle French admirable and partly from its etymon, Latin admirābilis. By surface analysis, admire + -able.

parole.significato: A positive emotion combining wonder and approbation; the regarding of another as being wonderful; a feeling of respect…

parole.significato: To be amazed at; to view with surprise; to marvel at.
parole.testo: From Middle English admyren, borrowed from Middle French admirer, from Latin admīror, from ad + mīror (“wonder at”).

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or at the age of adolescence; at the stage between being a child and an adult.
parole.testo: First attested ?1440, from Middle English adolescent, from Middle French adolescent or directly from Latin adolescentem, accusative form of adolescens, present participle of adolēscere (“to become adult, grow up”), from ad- (“to”) + alēscere (“to grow or become nourished”). parole.significato: To take (a child, heir, friend, citizen, etc.) by choice into a relationship.
parole.testo: From Middle French adopter, from Latin adoptō; ad + optō (“to choose, desire”), equivalent to ad- + opt.

parole.significato: Befitting of being adored; cute or loveable.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French adorable and its etymon Latin adōrābilis, from adōrāre + -bilis, from ad + ōrō. By surface analysis, adore + -able.

parole.significato: An act of religious worship.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French adoration, from Latin adōrātiō, adōrātiōnem (“worship, adoration”), from adōrō (“beseech; adore, worship”), from ad (“to, towards”) + ōrō (“beg”). From adore + -ation.

parole.significato: The process of adulterating.
parole.testo: From Middle French adulteration and its etymon Latin adulterātĭō. By surface analysis, adulterate + -ion.

parole.testo: From Middle French aduste, and its source, Latin adustus (“burnt, scorched”), past participle of adūrere.

parole.significato: The act of initiating hostilities or invasion.
parole.testo: From Middle French aggression, from Latin aggressio, from aggressus, past participle of aggredior (“to approach, address, attack”). By surface analysis, ag- + -gress + -ion.

parole.significato: The quality of being agile; the power of moving the limbs quickly and easily; quickness of motion
parole.testo: From late Middle English, borrowed from Middle French agilité, from Latin agilitās, from agilis (“nimble, fleet, quick”), equivalent to agile + -ity.

parole.significato: Of, or relating to, the ownership, tenure and cultivation of land.
parole.testo: From Middle French agrarien, from Latin agrarius (“of the land”), from stem of ager (“field”) + -arius.

parole.significato: The art or science of cultivating the ground, including the growing and harvesting of crops, and the rearing and manage…
parole.testo: From Middle English agriculture, partly from Middle French agriculture and partly from its etymon Latin agricultūra, from ager (“field”) + cultūra (“cultivation”). See acre and culture.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Alexandria.
parole.testo: Partly from Middle French alexandrin and partly from Latin Alexandrīnus.

parole.significato: An assertion, especially an accusation, not necessarily based on facts.

parole.testo: From Middle French allodial, and its source, Latin allōdiālis (“held in freehold”), from allōdium.

parole.significato: A metal that is a combination of two or more elements, at least one of which is a metal, a base metal.

parole.significato: To refer to something indirectly or by suggestion; to invoke it by implication rather than mention.

parole.significato: Relating to a choice between two or more possibilities.

parole.significato: Friendly, pleasant.

parole.significato: Having or showing ambition; wanting a lot of power, honor, respect, superiority, or other distinction.

parole.significato: Pleasant; agreeable.

parole.significato: Pleasantness.

parole.significato: Friendly, amicable.

parole.significato: Articles used in charging firearms and ordnance of all kinds; as powder, balls, shot, shells, percussion caps, rockets,…

parole.significato: Forgetfulness; cessation of remembrance of wrong; oblivion.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French amnestie (Modern French amnistie), a borrowing from Latin amnestia, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀμνηστία (amnēstía).

parole.significato: To remove forcibly.

parole.significato: A fully sufficient or abundant quantity of; enough or more than enough.
parole.testo: From late Middle English ample, from Middle French ample, from Latin amplus (“large”).

parole.significato: The measure of the size of something, especially its width or breadth; largeness, magnitude.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French amplitude, from Latin amplitūdō, from amplus (“large”). By surface analysis, ample + -itude.

parole.significato: surgical removal of all or part of a limb, etc.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to analogy.
parole.testo: From Middle French analogique, from Latin analogicus.

parole.significato: The herb dill; also dillseed.

parole.significato: To place (something) at an angle.

parole.significato: A criticism, a critical remark.

parole.significato: The record of a single event or item.

parole.significato: The act of destroying or otherwise turning into nothing, or nonexistence.

parole.significato: Not according to normality; abnormal.
parole.testo: From Middle French anormal and probably also partly Latin anōrmālis, equivalent to a- + normal.

parole.significato: Of, from, or pertaining to Antarctica and the south polar regions.

parole.significato: The act of anticipating, taking up, placing, or considering something beforehand, or before the proper time in natural…
parole.testo: From Middle English anticipacioun, from Middle French anticipation and its etymon Latin anticipātiō, anticipātiōnem. By surface analysis, anticipate + -ion.

parole.significato: The point, in an orbit about the Earth, that is farthest from the Earth: the apoapsis of an Earth orbiter.
parole.testo: From Middle French apogée, from Latin apogaeum, apogēum, from Ancient Greek ἀπόγειον (apógeion, “away from Earth”), from ἀπό (apó, “away”) + γῆ (gê, “Earth”).

parole.significato: An act of becoming visible; appearance; visibility.
parole.testo: From Middle French apparition, from Latin apparitio, from appareo.

parole.testo: From Middle English apposicioun, from Middle French apposition, from Latin appositiō, past participle of appōnere (“to put near”).

parole.significato: Relating to water; living in or near water, taking place in water.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French aquatique (“living in water”), from Latin aquaticus (“relating to water”), from aqua (“water”).

parole.significato: The son or male-line grandson of an emperor of the Austro-Hungarian Empire.

parole.significato: A professional who designs buildings or other structures, or who prepares plans and superintends construction.

parole.significato: A detachment of soldiers; soldiers collectively.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French armature, from Latin armātūra (“armour”). Doublet of armor and armure.

parole.significato: Crafty deception.

parole.significato: Someone who is skilled in their trade; an artisan.

parole.significato: A person who does not believe in deities or gods.
parole.testo: From Middle French athéiste (athée + -iste), from Latin atheos, from Ancient Greek ἄθεος (átheos, “godless, without god”), from ἀ- (a-, “without”) + θεός (theós, “god”).

parole.significato: Having to do with athletes.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French athletique and Latin āthlēticus, from Ancient Greek ἀθλητικός (athlētikós, “relating to an athlete”), from ἀθλητής (athlētḗs, “athlete”): equivalent to athlete + -ic. parole.significato: An extremely cruel act; a horrid act of injustice.
parole.testo: From Middle French atrocité, from Latin atrōcitās, from atrōx (“terrible, cruel”) + -tās, from āter (“matte black”).

parole.significato: To affirm to be correct, true, or genuine.

parole.significato: A thing that serves to bear witness, confirm, or authenticate; validation, verification, documentation.
parole.testo: From Middle French attestation, from Latin attestātiō; by surface analysis, attest + -ation.

parole.significato: The act of attributing something.
parole.testo: From Middle French attribution, from Latin attributio.

parole.significato: A group of people within hearing; specifically, a large gathering of people listening to or watching a performance, spe…
parole.testo: From Middle English audience, from Middle French audience, from Old French audience, from Latin audientia, from present participle audiēns (“hearing”), from verb audiō (“to hear”). Doublet of audiencia.

parole.significato: A performance, by an aspiring performer, to demonstrate suitability or talent.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French audicion, from Latin audītiō, from audiō (“to hear”).

parole.significato: That which augments.
parole.testo: From Middle English augmentatif, from Middle French augmentatif and its etymon Latin augmentātīvus, from augmentō. By surface analysis, augment + -ative.

parole.significato: Patronage or protection.
parole.testo: From Middle French auspice, from Latin auspicium, in turn from auspex.

parole.significato: Traditionally the third of the four seasons, when deciduous trees lose their leaves, and temperatures and daylight hour…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English autumpne, from Middle French automne, from Old French automne, autonne, from Latin autumnus. Some of the verbal senses are from Latin autumnāre.

parole.significato: Supreme, utmost bliss and happiness.
parole.testo: From Middle English beatitude, beatytude, from Middle French béatitude, from Latin beātitūdō (“happiness, blessedness”), from beātus (“happy, blessed”).

parole.significato: The state of being benign.
parole.testo: From Middle English benignite, from Middle French benignité (modern French bénignité), from Latin benignitās. By surface analysis, benign + -ity.

parole.significato: A great-grandfather.
parole.testo: From Middle French besaieul, besayel, from Old French beseel, from Latin bis (“twice”) + aviolus, diminutive of avus (“grandfather”).

parole.significato: A collection of books or treatises.
parole.testo: From Middle French bibliotheque, from Latin bibliothēca, from Ancient Greek βιβλιοθήκη (bibliothḗkē). Doublet of bibliotheca.

parole.significato: A bitter brownish-yellow or greenish-yellow secretion produced by the liver, stored in the gall bladder, and discharged…
parole.testo: From Middle French bile, from Latin bīlis (“bile”). Partially displaced native English gall (“bile”), from Middle English galle, from Old English galla, ġealla (“gall, bile”).

parole.significato: A large, wild bovid of the genus Bison.
parole.testo: From Middle English bysontes, bysountes pl, from Middle French bison, from Latin bisōn, bisōnt- (“wild ox”). parole.significato: A medieval primitive cannon, used chiefly in sieges for throwing heavy stone balls.
parole.testo: From Middle English bombard, from Middle French bombarde (“a bombard, mortar, catapult"; also "a bassoon-like musical instrument”), from Latin bombus (“buzzing; booming”). The modern pronunciation is from modern French bombarde.

parole.significato: A part or division of the intestines, usually the large intestine.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French bouel, from Old French boïel, from Latin botellus, diminutive of botulus (“sausage”). Doublet of boyau.

parole.significato: Without reason or intelligence (of animals).
parole.testo: From Middle French brut, from Old French brut, from Latin brūtus (“dull, stupid, insensible”), an Oscan loanword, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷréh₂us (“heavy”). Cognate with Ancient Greek βαρύς (barús), Persian گران (gerân) and Sanskrit गुरु (gurú) (English guru).

parole.significato: A purse.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French bourse, from Old French borse, from Latin bursa, from Ancient Greek βύρσα (búrsa). Doublet of purse, compare French bourse (“purse, fund”).

parole.significato: A cask or barrel.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French cade (“barrel”), from Latin cadus (“bottle, jar”).

parole.significato: caducous.
parole.testo: From Middle French caduc, from Latin cadūcus (“falling; transitory”).

parole.significato: An event resulting in great loss.
parole.testo: From Middle French calamité, from Latin calamitās (“loss, damage; disaster”).

parole.significato: Dark, obscure; murky.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French caligineux (“misty; obscure”), or directly from its Latin etymon cālīginōsus (“misty; dark, obscure”). Cālīginōsus is derived from cālīgō, cālīginis (“fog, mist, vapour; darkness, gloom”)) + -ōsus (suffix meaning ‘full of, prone to’ forming adjectives from nouns).

parole.significato: An artificial waterway or artificially improved river used for travel, shipping, or irrigation.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French canal, from Old French canal, from Latin canālis (“channel, canal, narrow passage”), from canna (“reed, cane”), from Ancient Greek κάννα (kánna, “reed”), from Akkadian 𒄀 (qanû, “reed”). Doublet of channel. See also cane and -al.

parole.significato: That captures; especially, (of an argument, words etc.) designed to capture or entrap in misleading arguments; sophisti…
parole.testo: From Middle English capcious, from Middle French captieux, or its source, Latin captiōsus, from captiō.

parole.significato: An act of capturing; a seizing by force or stratagem.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French capture (noun), from Latin captūra. Displaced native Old English fenġ (noun) and ġefōn (verb).

parole.significato: Pertaining to the heart.
parole.testo: From Middle French cardiaque, from Latin cardiacus, from Ancient Greek καρδιακός (kardiakós, “relating to the heart”), from καρδία (kardía, “heart”); by surface analysis, cardi- + -ac.

parole.significato: Of fundamental importance; crucial, pivotal.
parole.testo: From Middle French cardinal, from Latin cardinālis (“pertaining to a hinge, hence applied to that on which something turns or depends, important, principal, chief”), from cardin-, cardō (“hinge”) + -ālis, adjectival suffix.

parole.significato: A vegetable with a nutritious, juicy, sweet root that is often orange in colour, Daucus carota, family Apiaceae, especi…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English karette and Middle French carotte, both from Latin carōta, from Ancient Greek καρωτόν (karōtón). Doublet of carotte and related to caraway. parole.significato: A sculpted female figure serving as an architectural support taking the place of a column or a pillar supporting an ent…

parole.significato: A hat made from the fur of the beaver.
parole.testo: From Middle French castor, from Old French castor (“beaver”), from Latin castor (“beaver”), from Ancient Greek κάστωρ (kástōr), from Doric Greek κάστον (káston, “wood”).

parole.significato: A device or weapon for throwing or launching large objects.
parole.testo: From Middle French catapulte, from Latin catapulta, from Ancient Greek καταπέλτης (katapéltēs), from κατά (katá, “downwards, into, against”) + πάλλω (pállō, “to poise or sway a missile before it is thrown”). Doublet of catapulta.

parole.significato: To stop.
parole.testo: From Middle English cesen, cessen, from Middle French cesser (“to cease”), from Latin cessō (“leave off”), frequentative of cēdō (“to leave off, go away”). Compare secede.

parole.significato: To give up; yield to another.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French ceder, from Old French ceder, from Latin cēdō (“to yield”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱyesdʰ- (“to drive away; to go away”). Cognate with Tocharian B kätk- (“to cross, pass”).

parole.significato: A scroll, written document, or schedule.
parole.testo: From Middle English cedule, from Middle French cedule (modern French cédule), from Old French cedule, from Latin schedula. Doublet of schedule.

parole.significato: Synonym of centurion: An officer overseeing 100 men, especially (historical) in the Roman army.
parole.testo: From Middle English centener, centiner, centyner, from Middle French centenier, from Latin centēnārius (“containing 100”), q.v.

parole.significato: The point in the interior of a circle that is equidistant from all points on the circumference.
parole.testo: From Middle English center, centre, from Middle French centre, from Latin centrum, from Ancient Greek κέντρον (kéntron), from κεντεῖν (kenteîn, “to prick, goad”). Doublet of centrum. * (group theory): In the notation Z(G), the letter Z derives from the German Zentrum (“center”).

parole.significato: Australia, UK, Canada, Ireland, New Zealand, and South Africa standard spelling of center.
parole.testo: From Middle English center, centre, from Middle French centre, from Latin centrum, from Ancient Greek κέντρον (kéntron), from κεντεῖν (kenteîn, “to prick, goad”). Doublet of centrum.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the head.
parole.testo: From Middle French céphalique, from Latin cephalicus (“head”), from Ancient Greek κεφαλικός (kephalikós, “capital”), from κεφαλή (kephalḗ, “head”).

parole.significato: A ceasing or discontinuance, for example of an action, whether temporary or final.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French cessation, itself a borrowing from Latin cessātiō. By surface analysis, cease + -ation. Compare cession < cede.

parole.significato: That which is ceded.
parole.testo: From Middle French cession, from Latin cessionem, from past participle of cēdere (“to yield”). By surface analysis, cede + -sion.

parole.significato: The investing of money into a third party's lawsuit in which one has no vested interest.
parole.testo: From Middle English champartie, from Middle French champart (“field rent (portion of produce of field paid to feudal lord)”), probably from Latin campī (“fields”) + pars (“part”).

parole.significato: An edible leafy vegetable, Beta vulgaris subsp. cicla, with a slightly bitter taste.
parole.testo: From earlier card (remodelled after chardoon, obsolete form of cardoon), from Middle French carde, from Latin carduus (“thistle”). Doublet of cardoon.

parole.significato: Synonym of palmistry: fortune-telling performed by reading another's hand.

parole.significato: A thing; personal property.
parole.testo: From Middle French chose, from Latin causa (“cause, reason”). Doublet of cause.

parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English circumspeccioun, from Middle French circonspection or its etymon Latin circumspectio. By surface analysis, circum- + Latin spect + -ion, "looking [all] around" (as compared with the opposite concept, embodied as tunnel vision or blinders).

parole.significato: A goldish-yellow colour, like that of a lemon.
parole.testo: From Middle English citrine, partly from Middle French citrine and partly from Latin citrīnus.

parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French clavicule, from Latin clāvicula (“a small key”), diminutive of clāvis (“a key”).

parole.significato: A symbol found on a musical staff that indicates the pitches represented by the lines and the spaces on the staff
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French clef, from Latin clāvis (“a key”). Doublet of clave and clavis.

parole.significato: The precipitation of suspended particles as they increase in size by any of several physical or chemical processes.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French coagulation, from Latin coagulatio, coagulationem. Morphologically coagulate + -ion.

parole.significato: The act of coalescing.
parole.testo: From Middle French coalescence and its etymon Latin coalēscentia. Doublet of coalescency. By surface analysis, coalesce + -ence.

parole.significato: An addition or supplement that explains, modifies, or revokes a will or part of one.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French codicille, from Latin cōdicillus, diminutive of cōdex. See code.

parole.significato: The quality of cohering, or being coherent; internal consistency.
parole.testo: From Middle French coherence, from Latin cohaerentia. By surface analysis, cohere + -ence.

parole.significato: Unified; sticking together; making up a whole.
parole.testo: From Middle French coherent, from Latin cohaērēns, from co- + haereō. By surface analysis, cohere + -ent.

parole.significato: A fellow member of a profession, staff, academic faculty or other organization; an associate, a workmate.
parole.testo: From Middle French collegue, from Latin collēga (“a partner in office”), from com- (“with”) + lēgō (“to send on an embassy”), from lēx (“law”).

parole.significato: Formed by gathering or collecting; gathered into a mass, sum, or body.
parole.testo: From Middle French collectif, from Latin collēctīvus, from collēctus, past participle of colligō (“to collect”), from com- (“together”) + legō (“to gather”). Compare French collectif. Doublet of colectivo.

parole.significato: An academic institution.
parole.testo: From Middle English college, from Middle French college, from Old French college, from Latin collēgium. Doublet of collegium.

parole.significato: To burn up, to burn away, to consume with fire.
parole.testo: From Middle English combust (“burnt”), from Middle French combust, from Latin combustus, the perfect passive participle of Latin combūrere (“to burn up, to burn away”, transitive), whence also English combure. The verb was originally transitive.

parole.significato: Capable of burning.
parole.testo: From Middle French combustible [from combust (past participle of comburir) + -ible] and Latin combustibilis. By surface analysis, combust + -ible.

parole.significato: Feasting, banqueting.
parole.testo: From Middle English comessacoun, comessacyoun, commessacion, commessacioun, from Middle French comessacion and its etymon Latin cōmessātiō, cōmissātiō.

parole.significato: Worthy of commendation; deserving praise; admirable, creditable, or meritorious.
parole.testo: From Middle English commendable, from Middle French commendable, from Latin commendabilis, from commendare (“to commend, intrust to”), from com- + mandare (“to commit, intrust, enjoin”), from manus (“hand”) + dare (“to put”).

parole.significato: A series of comments or annotations; especially, a book of explanations or expositions on the whole or a part of some o…
parole.testo: From Middle French commentaire, from Latin commentārius, commentārium (“notebook”), compare French commentaire. See comment.

parole.significato: The exchange or buying and selling of commodities; especially the exchange of merchandise, on a large scale, between di…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French commerce, from Latin commercium. Doublet of comess.

parole.significato: The action of mixing or blending together; commingling.
parole.testo: From Middle English commixtion, from Middle French commixtion, and its source, Latin commixtiōnem, from commiscēre (“to mix”).

parole.significato: Ordinary sensible understanding; one's basic intelligence which allows for plain understanding and without which good d…
parole.testo: Calque of Middle French sens commun and its source, Latin sēnsus commūnis, itself a calque of Ancient Greek κοινὴ αἴσθησις (koinḕ aísthēsis).

parole.significato: A state of turbulent motion.
parole.testo: From Middle French commocion, from Latin commōtiōnem, accusative singular of commōtiō, from commoveō + -tiō.

parole.significato: Closely packed or densely constituted; having much material in a small volume.
parole.testo: From Middle French compact, from Latin compāctus, perfect passive participle of compingō (“join together”), from com- (“together”) + pangō (“fasten”), from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂ǵ- (“to attach, fix, fasten”).

parole.significato: Able to be compared (to).
parole.testo: From Middle English comparable, from Middle French comparable, from Latin comparābilis. By surface analysis, compare + -able.

parole.significato: The equal or peer of someone else; a close companion or associate.
parole.testo: From Middle English comper, from Middle French comper, from Latin compater, compatrem. Doublet of compere as well as compadre and goombah. Influenced by folk-etymological analysis as com- + peer.

parole.significato: To drive together, round up.
parole.testo: From Middle English compellen, borrowed from Middle French compellir, from Latin compellere, itself from com- (“together”) + pellere (“to drive”). Displaced native Old English nīedan.

parole.significato: To be in battle or in a rivalry with another for the same thing, position, or reward; to contend.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French competer, from Latin competere (“to coincide, to be equal to, to be capable of”), from com- (“with”) + petō (“to seek; to aim for, strive for”). Compare Latin competītor (“competitor”).

parole.significato: A person or organization against whom one is competing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French compétiteur, from Latin competitor.

parole.significato: The act or process of compiling or gathering together from various sources.
parole.testo: English compile + -ation, from Middle French, from Latin compilatio (“a raking together, a plundering, a collection of documents”).

parole.significato: to convince
parole.testo: From Middle French complaire, from Latin complaceō.

parole.significato: The act or process of complicating.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French complication, from Latin complicatio, complicationem. Morphologically complicate + -ion.

parole.significato: Made up of multiple components; compound or complex.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French composite, from Latin compositus, past participle of compōnō (“put together”). Doublet of compost, compote, and kompot.

parole.significato: Compost, composted manure.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French composture (“compost”), from late Old French composture, possibly from Latin compositūra, compostūra (“composition”); equivalent to compost + -ure. Compare Portuguese compostura, Spanish compostura.

parole.significato: Composed of elements; not simple.
parole.testo: From Middle English compounen, from Middle French componre, compondre (“to put together”), from Latin componō, from Latin com- (“together”) + ponō (“to put”).

parole.significato: A thorough understanding.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French compréhension, from Latin comprehēnsiō (“taking together”), from com- (“with, together”) + prehendō (“take”).

parole.significato: An increase in density; the act of compressing, or the state of being compressed; compaction.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French compression, from Latin compressiō, equivalent to compress + -ion.

parole.significato: The act or process of computing; calculation; reckoning.
parole.testo: From late Middle English computacioun, from Middle French computation, from Latin computatiō, from computare (“sum up, reckon, compute”); see compute. Morphologically compute + -ation.

parole.significato: An abstract and general idea; an abstraction.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French concept, from Latin conceptus (“a thought, purpose, also a conceiving, etc.”), from concipiō (“to take in, conceive”). Doublet of conceit and concetto. See conceive.

parole.significato: The act of conceding.
parole.testo: From late Middle English concession, from Middle French concession, from Latin concessiō (“a grant, permission, conceding”), from concēdō. Doublet of concessio.

parole.significato: The set of apartments in which cardinals are secluded while the process to elect a pope takes place.
parole.testo: PIE word  *ḱóm The noun is derived from Late Middle English conclave (“private chamber; (Roman Catholicism) private room where election of the Pope takes place; meeting held for this purpose”), borrowed from Middle French conclave (modern French conclave), or directly from its etymon Latin conclāve

parole.significato: Accompanying; conjoining; attending; concurrent.
parole.testo: First attested 1607; from Middle French concomitant, from Latin concomitāns, the present participle of concomitor (“to accompany”), from con- (“together”) + comitor (“to accompany”), from comes (“companion”).

parole.significato: A large open space in or in front of a building where people can gather, particularly one joining various paths, as in…
parole.testo: From Middle English concours, from Middle French concours and its etymon Latin concursus, concursum, from concurrere (“to run together”). See concur. Doublet of concours.

parole.significato: Greatly to be desired or lusted after; exciting concupiscence.
parole.testo: From Middle English concupiscibill, concupiscibl, concupiscible, concupyscyble, concupyssible, from Middle French concupiscible and its etymon, Latin concupīscibilis.

parole.significato: To concentrate toward the essence by making more close, compact, or dense, thereby decreasing size or volume.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French condenser, from Latin condēnsō.

parole.significato: One who conducts or leads; a guide; a director.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French conductour, from Old French conduitor, from Latin conductor.

parole.significato: A union or alliance of states or political organizations.
parole.testo: From Middle English confederacion, confideracion and Middle French confédération, from Old French confederacion, from Latin cōnfoederātiō. Doublet of confederacy.

parole.significato: To grant as a possession; to bestow.
parole.testo: From Early Modern English conferre, from Middle French conférer, from Old French conferer, from Latin cōnferō. parole.significato: Very sure of something; positive.
parole.testo: From Middle French confident, from Latin confidens (“confident, i.e. self-confident, in a good or bad sense, bold, daring, audacious, impudent”), present participle of confidere (“to trust fully, confide”). See confide.

parole.significato: The form of a thing, as depending on the relative placement of the parts of a thing's shape.
parole.testo: From Middle French configuration, from Latin cōnfigūrātiō. Morphologically configure + -ation.

parole.significato: A large fire extending to many objects, or over a large space; a general burning.
parole.testo: From Middle French, from Latin cōnflagrātiō (“burning, conflagration”).

parole.significato: To show (something or someone) to be false or wrong; to disprove or refute.
parole.testo: From Middle French confuter, from Latin confūtō.

parole.significato: The act or process of passing, or causing to pass, from a fluid to a solid state, as by the abstraction of heat; the ac…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French congelation (compare modern congélation), from Latin congelatio, congelationem, from congelo.

parole.significato: The act of congratulating.
parole.testo: From Middle English congratulacion, from Middle French congratulation or its etymon Latin congrātulātiō, from congrātulor (“to congratulate”). By surface analysis, congratulate + -ion.

parole.significato: Of or relating to marriage, or the relationship of spouses; connubial.
parole.testo: From Middle French conjugal, from Latin coniugālis (“con- + iugum ('yoke')”).

parole.significato: Conjuring, legerdemain or magic.
parole.testo: From Middle English conjuracioun, from Middle French conjuration, from Old French conjuracion, from Latin coniuratio (“a swearing together, a conspiracy”).

parole.significato: A consanguineous or family relationship through parentage or descent.
parole.testo: From Middle English consanguinite, consanguinyte, consanguinytee, consanguynyte, consangwinyte, from Middle French consanguinéité, consanguinité (from Old French consanguinité) and its etymon Latin cōnsanguinitās (accusative cōnsanguinitātem), from cōnsanguineus + -itās, from Latin com- (“together”)

parole.significato: Involuntary labor, especially military service, demanded by some established authority.
parole.testo: From Middle French conscription, from Latin cōnscriptiō (“levying of troops”).

parole.significato: Following as a result, inference, or natural effect.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French conséquent, from Latin consequens, consequentem, present participle of consequi (“to follow”), from con- + sequi (“to follow”). Compare French conséquent.

parole.significato: A person who favors maintenance of the status quo.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French conservatif, from Latin cōnservō (“to preserve”). Equivalent to conserve + -ative.

parole.significato: To think about seriously.
parole.testo: From Middle English consideren, from Middle French considerer, from Latin considerare.

parole.significato: To transfer to the custody of, usually for sale, transport, or safekeeping.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French consigner or directly from Latin cōnsignō (“furnish with a seal”), from con- + signō (“mark, sign”).

parole.significato: To be.
parole.testo: From Middle French consister, from Latin consistō (“stand together, stop, become hard or solid, agree with, continue, exist”), from com- (“together”) + sistō (“to cause to stand, stand”).

parole.significato: A form of rhyme having the same consonants but different vowels.
parole.testo: From Middle English consonance, from Middle French consonance, from Latin cōnsonantia. Doublet of consonancy. By surface analysis, con- + son- + -ance.

parole.significato: The spouse of a monarch.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French, ultimately from Latin cōnsors. As “companion or partner”, via Middle English consorte.

parole.significato: Agreement or concurrence for some end or purpose.
parole.testo: From Middle English conspiracioun, from Middle French conspiration, from Latin cōnspīrātiō, cōnspīrātiōnem. Doublet of conspiracy.

parole.significato: Custom, familiarity.
parole.testo: From Middle English consuetude, from Middle French consuetude, from Old French consuetude, learnedly borrowed from Latin cōnsuētūdō. Doublet of costume, custom, and kastom.

parole.significato: A visit to consult somebody, such as a doctor; a consultation.
parole.testo: From Middle French consulter, from Latin cōnsultum, from cōnsultus, from cōnsulō.

parole.significato: The act of consulting.
parole.testo: From Middle French consultation, from Latin consultatio. Morphologically consult + -ation.

parole.significato: Marked by heated arguments or controversy.
parole.testo: From Middle French contentieux, from Latin contentiōsus (“quarrelsome, perverse”), from contentiō (“contention”), from contendere, past participle contentus (“to contend”). Equivalent to English contention + -ous.

parole.significato: Lack of interruption or disconnection; the quality of being continuous in space or time.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French continuité, from Latin continuitas. By surface analysis, continu(e) + -ity.

parole.significato: The act or result of contorting; the state of being contorted: the twisting of something, especially oneself.
parole.testo: Derived from Middle French contortion, from Latin contortiō.

parole.significato: To draw together or nearer; to shorten, narrow, or lessen.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Middle French contracter, from Latin contractum, past participle of contrahere (“to bring together, to bring about, to conclude a bargain”), from con- (“with, together”) + trahere (“to draw, to pull”). The verb developed after the noun, and originally meant only "draw toget

parole.significato: To act contrary to an order; to fail to conform to a regulation or obligation.
parole.testo: From Middle French contravenir (French contrevenir), from Latin contraveniō.

parole.significato: controversy
parole.testo: From Middle French controversion and its etymon Latin contrōversiō.

parole.significato: Synonym of bruise.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French contusion, from Latin contūsiōnem, accusative singular of contūsiō, from contūsus, past participle of contundō (“to beat”), by surface analysis, com- + tundō.

parole.significato: To come together; to meet; to unite.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French convenir, from Latin convenio, convenire (“come together”), from con- (“with, together”) + veniō (“come”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷm̥yéti, from the root *gʷem-.

parole.significato: A meeting or gathering.
parole.testo: Recorded since about 1440, borrowed from Middle French convention, from Latin conventiō (“meeting, assembling; agreement, convention”), from conveniō (“come, gather or meet together, assemble”), from con- (“with, together”) + veniō (“come”). Equivalent to convene + -tion.

parole.significato: Curved or bowed outward like the outside of a bowl, circle, or sphere.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French convexe, from Latin convexus (“arched”).

parole.significato: To convene, to cause to assemble for a meeting.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French convoquer, from Latin convocare, from con- (“with”) + vocō (“to call”). Doublet of convocate.

parole.significato: The act of coupling or joining; union; conjunction.
parole.testo: From Middle French copulation, from Latin copulo (“to join, unite, connect”).

parole.significato: The white headdress worn by the Sisters of Charity.
parole.testo: From Middle French cornette, diminutive of corne, from Latin cornua (“horns”).

parole.significato: A small crown, such as is worn by a noble.
parole.testo: From Middle French couronnette, from Old French coronete, diminutive of corone (“crown”), from Latin corona, from Ancient Greek κορώνη (korṓnē, “a type of sea-bird, perhaps shearwater; a crow; anything curved or hooked (like a door handle or the tip of a bow); a type of crown”).

parole.significato: To be equivalent or similar in character, quantity, quality, origin, structure, function etc.
parole.testo: From Middle French correspondre, from Latin com- (“with”) + respondeo (“to match, to answer to”), equivalent to co- + respond.

parole.significato: A fellow rival; a competitor; a rival.
parole.testo: From Middle French corrival, from Latin corrīvālis.

parole.significato: A diminutive of the bendlet, containing one half its area or one quarter the area of the bend: a thin line borne around…
parole.testo: From Middle French cotice, costice, from côte + -ice, from Latin costa (“rib”).

parole.significato: To bend; to bow.
parole.testo: From Middle English courben, from Middle French courber, from Latin curvō. Doublet of curb.

parole.significato: Believable or plausible.
parole.testo: From Middle English credible, borrowed from Middle French credible, from Latin crēdibilis (“worthy of belief”), from crēdō (“believe”); see credit.

parole.significato: To believe; to put credence in.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French crédit (“belief, trust”), from Latin crēditum (“a loan, credit”), neuter of crēditus, past participle of crēdere (“to believe”). The verb is from the noun. Doublet of shraddha, creed.

parole.significato: A willingness to believe in someone or something in the absence of reasonable proof; credulousness.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English credulite (“faith, belief”), borrowed from Middle French credulité (French crédulité), from Latin crēdulitās. Corresponding to credulous + -ity (compare credulosity).

parole.significato: Twilight.
parole.testo: From Middle French crepuscule m, ultimately from Latin crepusculum n. Doublet of crepuscle and crepusculum.

parole.significato: To criticise.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French critique, from Latin criticus, from Ancient Greek κριτικός (kritikós, “of or for judging, able to discern”), from κρίνω (krínō, “to judge”).

parole.significato: The state of being crude.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French crudité, from Latin crūditās. By surface analysis, crude + -ity. Doublet of crudité.

parole.significato: Any member of the family Cucurbitaceae of gourds.
parole.testo: From Middle English cocurbite, concurbite, cucurbita, cucurbite, from Middle French cucurbite and Latin cucurbita. Doublet of gourd.

parole.significato: A component of armor, consisting of overlapping plates designed to protect the buttocks.
parole.testo: From Middle French culet, diminutive of cul (“bottom”), from Latin culus (“arse”).

parole.significato: to maintain in an environment suitable for growth (especially of bacteria) (compare cultivate)
parole.testo: From Middle French culture (“cultivation; culture”), from Latin cultūra (“cultivation; culture”), from cultus, perfect passive participle of colō (“till, cultivate, to grow, worship”) (related to colōnus and colōnia), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷel- (“to move; to turn (around)”).

parole.significato: A concrete margin along the edge of a road; a kerb (UK, Australia, New Zealand).
parole.testo: From Middle French courbe (“curve, curved object”), from Latin curvus (“bent, crooked, curved”). Doublet of curve.

parole.significato: Pertaining to a court; courtly.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French curial, from Latin cūriālis.

parole.significato: Hasty or superficial.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French cursoire (“rapid”), from Latin cursorius (“hasty, of a race or running”).

parole.significato: A surface created by projecting a closed two-dimensional curve along an axis intersecting the plane of the curve.
parole.testo: From Middle French chilindre, cylindre, from Latin cylindrus, from Ancient Greek κύλινδρος (kúlindros), from κυλίνδω (kulíndō) "I roll or wallow" (intransitive). Doublet of calander and calender.

parole.significato: A person whose outlook is scornfully negative.
parole.testo: From Middle English cynike, cynicke, from Middle French cynique, from Latin cynicus, from Ancient Greek κυνικός (kunikós), originally derived from the portico in Athens called Κυνόσαργες (Kunósarges), the earliest home of the Cynic school, later reinterpreted as being derived from κύων (kúōn, “dog”)

parole.significato: The eldest son of the king of France. Under the Valois and Bourbon dynasties, the Dauphin of France, generally shortene…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English Dauphin, from Middle French dauphin, from Old French dalphin, from Latin delphīnus, from Ancient Greek δελφίς (delphís); the modern pronunciation is sometimes remodelled on Modern French. Doublet of dolphin.

parole.significato: Weak; feeble.
parole.testo: From Middle French débile (“weak”), from Latin dēbilis.

parole.significato: In bookkeeping, an entry in the left hand column of an account.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French debet, from Latin debitum (“what is owed, a debt”), neuter of debitus, past participle of debere (“to owe”); Doublet of debt.

parole.significato: Any set of rules that have the weight of authority
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French Décalogue, from Latin decalogus, from Ancient Greek δεκάλογος (dekálogos, from δέκα (déka, “ten”) + λόγος (lógos, “statement”)). Equivalent to deca- + -logue.

parole.significato: Appropriate; suitable for the circumstances.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French décent, or its source, Latin decēns, present participle of decet (“it is fitting or suitable”), from Proto-Indo-European *deḱ- (“to take, accept, to receive, greet, be suitable”) (compare Ancient Greek δοκέω (dokéō, “to appear, seem, think”), δέχομαι (dékhomai, “to accept

parole.significato: Likely or attempting to deceive.
parole.testo: From Middle French déceptif, from Latin dēceptīvus, from dēcipiō (“to deceive”).

parole.significato: The act of deciding.
parole.testo: Derived from Middle French, from Latin dēcīsiō, dēcīsiōnis, from dēcīdō (“to decide”).

parole.significato: To recite, e.g., poetry, in a theatrical way; to speak for rhetorical display; to speak pompously, noisily, or theatric…
parole.testo: From Middle French declamer, from Latin dēclāmō.

parole.significato: A falling off, decay or descent.
parole.testo: From late Middle English declinson, from Middle French declinaison (Modern French: déclinaison), from Latin dēclīnātiō. Doublet of declination.

parole.significato: At a given point, the angle between magnetic north and true north.
parole.testo: From Middle English declinacioun, borrowed from Middle French declination, from Latin declinatio. Doublet of declension.

parole.significato: Weakened or worn out from age or wear.
parole.testo: From Middle English decrepyt (ante 1439), from Middle French décrépit, from Latin dēcrepitus (“very old”), from crepō (“to creak”).

parole.significato: The state of being decrepit or worn out from age or long use.
parole.testo: From Middle French décrépitude, from Old French, from Latin dēcrepitūdō (“decrepitude”).

parole.significato: Decrepitude.
parole.testo: From Middle French décrépité, from Latin dēcrepitās.

parole.significato: That which is deducted; that which is subtracted or removed.
parole.testo: From Middle French déduction, from Latin deductio. Equivalent to deduct + -ion or deduce + -tion.

parole.significato: To submit to the opinion or desire of others in respect to their judgment or authority.
parole.testo: From late Middle English differren (“to refer for judgement”), from Middle French déférer, from Latin dēferō. Doublet of delate. See also infer, collate and confer, relate and refer, as well as prelate and prefer among others.

parole.significato: A duct in the body serving to carry away from, as opposed to an afferent one.
parole.testo: From Middle English defferent, from Middle French deferent (modern French déférent) or its etymon Latin dēferēns, dēferentis.

parole.significato: A statement of the meaning of a word, word group, sign, or symbol; especially, a dictionary definition.
parole.testo: From Middle English diffinicioun, from Middle French definition, from Latin dēfīnītiō, from dēfīniō. Equivalent to define + -ition.

parole.significato: Having an unusual and unattractive shape; deformed, misshapen; hence, hideous, ugly.
parole.testo: From Middle English deforme (“out of shape, deformed”) [and other forms], from Middle French deforme (modern French difforme (“misshapen, deformed”)), or directly from its etymon Latin dēfōrmis (“departing physically from the correct shape, deformed, malformed, misshapen, ugly; (figuratively) depart

parole.significato: The state of being deformed.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English deformite, from Middle French deformite, from Latin dēfōrmitās (“deformity, ugliness”), from dēfōrmis (“deformed, ugly”) + -itās, from dē + fōrma (“shape, form”).

parole.significato: divine; of or relating to a deity or deities.
parole.testo: From Middle French déifique, from Latin deificus, from deus (“god”) + facio (“to make”).

parole.significato: The act of deifying; exaltation to divine honors; apotheosis.
parole.testo: From Middle English deificacion, from Middle French deifier + -acion or borrowed directly from Latin deificātiō(n), from deific(ā) (“deify”) + -tiō(n) (noun suffix), from de(i) (“god”) + -ficō (“make”). By surface analysis, deif(y) + -ication. * In the Christian, theological sense, influenced by the

parole.significato: Synonym of divinity: the state, position, or fact of being a god.
parole.testo: From Middle French deité, from Latin deitās.

parole.significato: That deliberates, considers carefully.
parole.testo: From Middle French délibératif, from Latin deliberativus.

parole.significato: Late or failing to pay a debt or other financial obligation, like a mortgage or loan.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French délinquant, ultimately from Latin delinquens, present participle of delinquo.

parole.significato: The conveyance or transfer of an estate, either in fee for life or for years, most commonly the latter.
parole.testo: From Middle English demyse, dimise, dimisse, dymyse, from Middle French démise, the feminine singular past participle of démettre (“to put down, relinquish”); from Latin dēmissa, feminine singular of perfect passive participle of dēmittō. The "death" and "end" senses derive by way of euphemism from

parole.significato: To destroy (buildings, etc.), especially in a planned or intentional fashion.
parole.testo: Attested since the 16th century; from Middle French demoliss-, the stem of some conjugated forms of the verb demolir (“to destroy”, “to tear down”), from Latin dēmōlior (“to tear down”). Displaced native Old English tōweorpan (literally “to throw apart”).

parole.significato: That serves to demonstrate, show or prove.
parole.testo: From Middle English demonstratif, from Middle French démonstratif, from Latin dēmōnstrātīvus. Equivalent to demonstrate + -ive.

parole.significato: To demonstrate.
parole.testo: From Middle French demonstrer, from Old French demonstrer, demoustrer, from Latin dēmonstrō, with re-Latinized spelling.

parole.significato: To indicate; to mark.
parole.testo: From Middle French denoter, from Latin denotare, from de- (“complete”) and notare (“to mark out”).

parole.significato: Having relatively high density.
parole.testo: From Middle French dense, from Latin dēnsus, from Proto-Indo-European *dens- (“thick, dense”) (whence also Ancient Greek δασύς (dasús)).

parole.significato: The amount of a certain phenomenon (such as stuff, things, energy, or otherwise) in a given area (surface area) or volu…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French densité or Latin densitas. Morphologically dense + -ity.

parole.significato: The act of stripping off covering, or removing the surface; a making bare.
parole.testo: From Middle French dénudation, from Latin denudatio.

parole.significato: To divest of all covering; to make bare or naked; to strip.
parole.testo: From Middle French dénuder, from Latin dēnūdāre, from dē- + nūdus (“bare”).

parole.significato: Relying upon; depending upon.
parole.testo: From Middle English dependaunt, dependent, from Middle French dependant (present participle of dependre (“to depend”)) and Latin dēpendēns (present participle of dēpendeō (“to depend”)). By surface analysis, depend + -ent.

parole.significato: To bewail; to weep bitterly over; to feel sorrow for.
parole.testo: From Middle French déplorer, from Old French deplorer, from Latin dēplōrāre (“to lament over, bewail”), from dē- + plōrāre (“to wail, weep aloud”); origin uncertain.

parole.significato: Detraction; depreciation.
parole.testo: From Middle French dépravation, from Latin dēprāvātiō (“perversion, distortion, corruption, depravity”).

parole.significato: The act of deprecating.
parole.testo: From Middle French deprecation (French: déprécation), from Latin dēprecātiōnem, from dēprecātiō (“deprecation, invocation”), from dēprecor (“to avert, warn off; to deprecate”).

parole.significato: An act of consuming agricultural resources (crops, livestock), especially as plunder.
parole.testo: From Middle French déprédation, from Latin depraedatio.

parole.significato: A leading or drawing off of water from a stream or source.
parole.testo: From Middle English derivacioun, borrowed from Middle French dérivation, from Latin dērīvātiō, dērīvātiōnem. Morphologically derive + -ation.

parole.significato: Obtained by derivation; not radical, original, or fundamental.
parole.testo: From Middle French dérivatif, from Latin dērīvātus, perfect passive participle of dērīvō (“to derive”). Related to derive; by surface analysis, derive + -ative.

parole.significato: Descending; going down.
parole.testo: From Middle English dessendaunte, borrowed from Middle French, from Latin dēscendēns, present participle of descendere, from dē + scandere (“to climb, ascend”).

parole.significato: To cease to proceed or act; to stop (often with from).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French desister, from Latin dēsistō, from dē- + sistō (whence de-).

parole.significato: The act of desolating or laying waste; destruction of inhabitants; depopulation.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English desolacioun, from Middle French, Old French desolacion f, from Latin dēsōlātiō f.

parole.significato: Causing destruction; damaging.
parole.testo: From Middle English destructyve, from Middle French destructif, from Latin dēstrūctīvus, from past participle of dēstruere (“to tear down, destroy”) + -īvus.

parole.significato: The state when something (for example, a custom or a law) is no longer observed nor practised; disuse, obsolescence.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English desuetude, dissuetude (“discontinuance of a practice, disuse”), from Middle French désuétude (“obsolescence”) (modern French désuétude), from Latin dēsuētūdo (“discontinuance of a practice or a habit, disuse”), from dēsuētus + -tūdō (“suffix forming abstract nouns indicating

parole.significato: The act of detaining or the state of being detained; hindrance.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French détention, from Latin detentio, detentionem. Equivalent to detain + -tion.

parole.significato: To dislike (someone or something) intensely; to loathe.
parole.testo: PIE word  *tréyes From Middle French detester (French détester), from Latin dētestor (“to imprecate evil while calling the gods to witness", "denounce", "hate intensely”), from dē- + testor (“to testify, bear witness”), from testis (“a witness”); see test, testify. Doublet of detestate.

parole.significato: To take away; to withdraw or remove.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French détracter, from Latin detractum, past participle of detraho.

parole.significato: Duty, business; something that one must do.
parole.testo: From Middle English devoir, borrowed from Middle French devoir, from Old French deveir, from Latin dēbēre (“to owe; ought, must”).

parole.significato: Skill in performing tasks, especially with the hands.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French dextérité, from Latin dexteritas, from dexter (“on the right”), this is in reference to most people having greater fine motor skills in their right hand. Partially displaced native Old English handcræft, whence Modern English handcraft.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a deacon or the diaconate.
parole.testo: From Middle French diaconal, from Latin diaconus (“deacon”).

parole.significato: Joining two nonadjacent vertices (of a polygon or polyhedron).
parole.testo: From Middle French diagonal, from Latin diagōnālis, from Ancient Greek διαγώνιος (diagṓnios, “from angle to angle”), from διά (diá, “across”) + γωνία (gōnía, “angle”).

parole.significato: A graduated, circular scale over which a needle moves to show a measurement (such as speed).
parole.testo: The original meaning was 'sundial' and/or 'clock dial'; from Middle English diall, from Middle French dyal, from Latin diālis (“daily, concerning the day”), because of its use in telling the time of day, from Latin diēs (“day”). Compare Spanish dial and día (“day”).

parole.significato: A lect (often a regional or minority language) as part of a group or family of languages, especially if they are viewed…
parole.testo: From Middle French dialecte, from Latin dialectos, dialectus, from Ancient Greek διάλεκτος (diálektos, “conversation, the language of a country or a place or a nation, the local idiom which derives from a dominant language”), from διαλέγομαι (dialégomai, “to participate in a dialogue”), from διά (di

parole.significato: To spread (something) over or through as in air, water, or other matter, especially by fluid motion or passive means.
parole.testo: From Middle French diffuser, from Latin diffūsus, past participle of diffundere, from dis- + fundere.

parole.significato: Possible to discern; detectable or derivable by use of the senses or the intellect.
parole.testo: From Middle French discernable; spelling changed from -a- to -i- in the 17th century to conform to Latin discernibilis. By surface analysis, discern + -ible.

parole.significato: Verbal exchange, conversation.
parole.testo: From Middle English discours, borrowed from Middle French discours (“conversation, speech”), from Latin discursus (“the act of running about”), from Latin discurrō (“run about”), from dis- (“apart”) + currō (“run”). Spelling modified by influence of Middle French cours (“course”). Doublet of discurs

parole.significato: Of or concerning discourse.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French discursif, formed from the stem of Latin discursus and the suffix -if, and in part borrowed from Medieval Latin discursivus. By surface analysis, discourse + -ive.

parole.significato: To cause an intense dislike for something.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French desgouster, from Old French desgouster (“to put off one's appetite”), from des- (“dis-”) + gouster, goster (“to taste”), from Latin gustus (“a tasting”). By surface analysis, dis- + gust (“taste”). The noun is from Middle French desgoust, from the verb.

parole.significato: Not connected; separated.
parole.testo: From Middle English disjunctief, disjunctyf, from Middle French disjunctif and Latin disjunctīvus (“placed in opposition”).

parole.significato: A dime minted in 1792.
parole.testo: From Middle French dixme, Old French disme (“tenth, tithe”), from Latin decimus (“tenth”). Doublet of dime.

parole.significato: Absence of order; state of not being arranged in an orderly manner.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French desordre (modern French désordre), from Old French desordre, from des- + ordre; by surface analysis, dis- + order (<< Latin ōrdō). Compare typologically Russian непоря́док (neporjádok), беспоря́док (besporjádok), неуря́дица (neurjádica) (akin to ряд (rjad), поря́док (porj

parole.significato: The state of being unequal; difference.
parole.testo: From Middle French disparité, from Latin disparitātem, accusative of disparitās, from dispār + -tās, from dis- + pār. By surface analysis, dis- + parity.

parole.significato: To scatter in different directions.
parole.testo: From Middle French disperser, from Latin dispersus, past participle of dispergō (“to scatter abroad, disperse”), from dis- (“apart”) + spargō (“to scatter”); see sparse.

parole.significato: The way in which something or someone is disposed or disposed of (in any sense of those terms); thus:
parole.testo: From Middle English disposicioun, from Middle French disposition, from Latin dispositiōnem, accusative singular of dispositiō, from dispōnō. By surface analysis, dispose + -ition. Doublet of dispositio.

parole.significato: Intending to, resulting in, or capable of disposition (disposing, disposing of, or settling a matter).
parole.testo: From Middle French dispositif and its source, Latin dispositus. Compare Piedmontese dispositiv.

parole.significato: An act of expressing dissent, especially spoken.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English dissencioun, from Middle French dissention, discention, from Old French dissension, from Latin dissensio.

parole.significato: A harsh, discordant combination of sounds.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French dissonance, from Latin dissonantia; by surface analysis, dis- + son- + -ance.

parole.significato: To convince not to try or do.
parole.testo: From Middle French dissuader, from Latin dissuādeō (“to urge differently”, “to advise against”, “to dissuade”), from dis- (“away from”, “asunder”) + suādeō (“to recommend”, “to advise”, “to urge”).

parole.significato: Something that distracts.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French distraction, from Latin distractio. Equivalent to distract + -ion.

parole.significato: Relating to distribution.
parole.testo: From Middle French distributif, from Latin distribūtīvus.

parole.significato: A cash payment of money by a company to its shareholders, usually made periodically (e.g., quarterly or annually).
parole.testo: From Middle French dividende, from Latin dīvidendum (“thing to be divided”), future passive participle of dīvidō (“to divide”), by surface analysis, divide + -end.

parole.significato: To foretell (something), especially by the use of divination.
parole.testo: Replaced Middle English devine, devin from Middle French deviner, from Latin dīvīnō.

parole.significato: Ready to accept instruction or direction; obedient; subservient.
parole.testo: From Middle English docyle, from Middle French docile, from Latin docilis, from docēre (“teach”). Compare Portuguese dócil ("docile").

parole.significato: The quality of being docile.
parole.testo: From Middle French docilité, from Latin docilitas.

parole.significato: An original or official paper used as the basis, proof, or support of anything else, including any writing, book, or ot…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French document, from Latin documentum.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the home.
parole.testo: From Middle French domestique, from Latin domesticus, from domus (“house, home”).

parole.significato: A home or residence.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English domicelle, domicylie, from Middle French domicile and directly from Latin domicilium.

parole.significato: Power or the use of power; sovereignty over something; stewardship, supremacy.
parole.testo: From Middle English dominion, from Middle French dominion, from Latin dominium (“lordship, right of ownership”), from dominus (“lord”), from domus (“house”). See demain, demesne, domain, dominium.

parole.significato: A voluntary gift or contribution for a specific cause.
parole.testo: From Middle English donacion, donation, from Middle French donation, from Latin dōnātiō (“a present”), from dōnō (“to give”), from dōnum (“a gift”). Recorded in English since the 15th century. Equivalent to donate + -ion.

parole.significato: The process of falling asleep.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French dormition, from Latin dormītiōnem.

parole.significato: Dowry.
parole.testo: From Middle English dote (“endowment”) (c. 1450), from Middle French dote (modern dot), from Latin dos.

parole.significato: To endow, donate.
parole.testo: From Middle French doter, Latin dōtāre.

parole.significato: A widow holding property or title derived from her late husband.
parole.testo: From Middle French douagere, douagiere, from douage (“dower”), from the verb douer (“to endow”), from Latin dōtō (“to endow”), from dōs (“dowry”).

parole.significato: The process of doubting or the state of being in doubt; hesitation, uncertainty.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English dubytacion, from Middle French dubitation, from Latin dubitātiō.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a duke, a duchess, or the duchy or dukedom they hold.
parole.testo: From Middle French ducal, from Latin ducālis. Doublet of dogal.

parole.significato: Now chiefly home economics: the art or science of household management, especially relating to the appropriate organiza…
parole.testo: From economic (noun) (obsolete) + -s (suffix forming pluralia tantum, and regular plural forms of nouns). parole.significato: Poured out freely; profuse.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French effuser, from Latin effusus, past participle of effundere (“to pour out”).

parole.significato: A liquid outpouring.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French effusion, from Latin effūsiō (“outpouring”). Displaced native Old English āgotennes.

parole.significato: The act of ejecting.
parole.testo: From Middle French éjection, from Latin eiectio.

parole.significato: To pass or move by.
parole.testo: From Middle French elapser, from Latin elapsus.

parole.significato: Grace, refinement, and beauty in movement, appearance, or manners.
parole.testo: From Middle French élégance, from Latin ēlegantia (“exquisiteness; refinement, elegance”).

parole.significato: Characterised by or exhibiting elegance; having grace, refinement, or tasteful simplicity.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English elegaunt, from Middle French elegant, ultimately from Latin ēlegāns, collateral form of present participle of ēligere, from ex- (“out of, from”) + legō (“choose, select, appoint”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to an elegy.
parole.testo: From Middle French élégiaque, from Latin elegīacus, from Ancient Greek ἐλεγειακός (elegeiakós).

parole.significato: A mournful or plaintive poem; a funeral song; a poem of lamentation.
parole.testo: From Middle French elegie, from Latin elegīa, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἐλεγείᾱ (elegeíā), ellipsis of ἐλεγείᾱ ᾠδή (elegeíā ōidḗ, “an elegiac song”).

parole.significato: Allowed to and meeting the necessary conditions required to participate in or be chosen for something.
parole.testo: From Middle French eligible, from Latin eligibilis, from ēligō (“to select, to choose”).

parole.significato: To come into view.
parole.testo: First attested in the late 16th century. Borrowed from Middle French emerger, from Latin ēmergō (“to rise up or out”), from ē- (a variant of ex- (“out, forth”)) + mergō (“to dip, to sink”)

parole.significato: Noteworthy, remarkable, great.
parole.testo: From Middle French éminent, from Latin present participle ēminēns, ēminentis, from verb ēmineō (“to project, protrude”), from ex- (“out of, from”) + mineō, related to mons (English mount). parole.significato: Something which is emitted or sent out; issue.
parole.testo: First attested in 1607. From Middle French émission, from Latin ēmissiō (“sending forth”), from ēmittō (“send out”), from ex (“from, out of”) + mittō (“send”).

parole.significato: The occupation or work for which one is used, and often paid.
parole.testo: From employ (itself from Middle French employer, from Middle French empleier, from Latin implicō (“enfold, involve, be connected with”), itself from in- + plicō (“fold”)) + -ment.

parole.significato: The endeavor or desire to equal or excel someone else in qualities or actions.
parole.testo: From Middle French émulation, from Latin aemulātiō.

parole.significato: To amuse (someone); to engage the attention of agreeably.
parole.testo: From Middle English entertenen, from Middle French entretenir, from Old French entretenir, from entre (“among”) + tenir (“to hold”), from Latin inter + teneō (“hold, keep”). parole.significato: An extended narrative poem in elevated or dignified language, celebrating the feats of a deity, demigod (heroic epic),…
parole.testo: From Middle French épique, from Latin epicus, from Ancient Greek ἐπικός (epikós), from ἔπος (épos, “word, story”).

parole.significato: An inscription in stone.
parole.testo: From Middle French epigramme, from Latin epigramma, from Ancient Greek ἐπίγραμμα (epígramma, “inscription”).

parole.significato: A short speech, spoken directly at the audience at the end of a play
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French epilogue, from Latin epilogus, from Ancient Greek ἐπίλογος (epílogos, “a conclusion, peroration of a speech, epilogue of a play”), from ἐπιλέγω (epilégō, “to say in addition”). parole.significato: A term used to characterize a person or thing.
parole.testo: From Middle French épithète, from Latin epithetum, epitheton, from Ancient Greek ἐπίθετον (epítheton, “epithet, adjective”), the neuter of ἐπίθετος (epíthetos, “additional”), from ἐπιτίθημι (epitíthēmi, “to add on”), from ἐπι- (epi-, “in addition”) + τίθημι (títhēmi, “to put”) (suf. possibly related

parole.significato: The embodiment or encapsulation of a class of items.
parole.testo: From Middle French, from Latin epitomē, from Ancient Greek ἐπιτομή (epitomḗ, “an abridgment, also a surface-incision”), from ἐπιτέμνω (epitémnō, “to cut upon the surface, cut short, abridge”), from ἐπι- (epi-, “up”) + τέμνω (témnō, “to cut”).

parole.significato: The fact of being equal.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French equalité (modern French égalité), from Latin aequālitās, aequālitātem. Doublet of equity. By surface analysis, equal + -ity

parole.significato: Equipment or supplies, especially military ones.
parole.testo: From Middle French equippage, from equipper. The "carriage" sense may be influenced by Latin equus (“horse”).

parole.significato: The result of having been worn away or eroded, as by a glacier on rock or the sea on a cliff face.
parole.testo: From Middle French erosion, from Latin ērōsiō (“eating away”), derived from ērōdō. The first known occurrence in English was in the 1541 translation by Robert Copland of Guy de Chauliac's medical text The Questyonary of Cyrurygens. Copland used erosion to describe how ulcers developed in the mouth.

parole.significato: Containing an error; inaccurate.
parole.testo: From late Middle English erroneous, from Middle French erroneux, from Latin erroneus.

parole.significato: Profound knowledge acquired from learning and scholarship.
parole.testo: First attested in the 15th Century. From Middle French érudition, from Latin eruditio (“an instructing, learning, erudition”), from erudire (“to instruct, educate, cultivate”, literally “free from rudeness”), from e (“out”) + rudis (“rude”). By surface analysis, erudite + -ion.

parole.significato: A violent ejection, such as the spurting out of lava from a volcano.
parole.testo: From Middle French éruption, from Latin eruptio.

parole.significato: A written composition of moderate length, exploring a particular issue or subject.
parole.testo: Since late 16th century, borrowed from Middle French essay, essai (“essay”), meaning coined by Montaigne at the same time, from the same words with the earlier meanings 'experiment; assay; attempt', from Old French essay, essai, assay, assai, from Latin exagium (“weight; weighing, testing on the bal

parole.significato: The inherent nature of a thing or idea.
parole.testo: From Middle English essence, from Middle French essence, from Latin essentia (“the being or essence of a thing”), from an artificial formation of esse (“to be”), to translate Ancient Greek οὐσία (ousía, “being”), from ὤν (ṓn), present participle of εἰμί (eimí, “to be, exist”). Displaced native Old E

parole.significato: Assessment, estimation, or regard; especially; favourable estimation or regard.
parole.testo: First at end of 16th century; borrowed from Middle French estimer, borrowed from Latin aestimō. See estimate and aim, an older word, partly a doublet.

parole.significato: A strait or channel of the sea.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French euripe, from Latin eurīpus, from Ancient Greek Εὔρῑπος (Eúrīpos, “Euripus”).

parole.significato: To get away from by cunning; to avoid by using dexterity, subterfuge, address, or ingenuity; to cleverly escape from.
parole.testo: From Middle French évader, from Latin ēvādō (“to pass or go over; flee”), from ē (“out of, from”) + vādō (“to go; walk”). See also wade.

parole.significato: A wandering about, excursion, trip or a roving.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French evagation, evagacion or its etymon Latin ēvagātiō, from ēvagārī (“to wander forth”). See also vagary.

parole.significato: An occurrence; something that happens.
parole.testo: From Middle French event, from Latin ēventus (“an event, occurrence”), from ēveniō (“to happen, to fall out, to come out”), from ē (“out of, from”), short form of ex + veniō (“come”); related to venture, advent, convent, invent, convene, evene, etc.

parole.significato: To show or demonstrate clearly; to manifest.
parole.testo: From Middle French évincer, from Latin ēvincō (“conquer entirely, prevail over; prove exhaustively”), from ē- (short form of ex- (intensive prefix)) + vincō (“conquer”). Doublet of evict.

parole.significato: Possible to avoid; avertible.
parole.testo: From Middle French evitable (modern French évitable), from Latin ēvītābilis (“avoidable”), from ēvītō (“to avoid”) + -bilis (“-able”, able or worthy to be). parole.significato: To avoid.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French eviter, from Latin ēvītō (“to avoid”).

parole.significato: out of
parole.testo: From Middle English, from words borrowed from Middle French; from Latin ex (“out of, from”), from Proto-Indo-European *eǵ-, *eǵs- (“out”), *eǵʰs.
