parole.significato: The act of demanding with authority, and compelling to pay or yield; compulsion to give or furnish; a levying by force
parole.testo: From Middle English exaccioun, exaccion, from Middle French exaction, from Old French, from Latin exāctiō.

parole.significato: To exclude; to specify as being an exception.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French excepter, from Latin exceptus.

parole.significato: The removal of some text during editing.
parole.testo: From Middle French excision, from Latin excīsiō(n).

parole.significato: To cry out suddenly, from some strong emotion.
parole.testo: From Middle French exclamer, from Latin exclāmō, exclāmāre (“call out”), from ex- + clāmō (“to call”).

parole.significato: A loud calling or crying out, for example as in surprise, pain, grief, joy, anger, etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French exclamation, from Latin exclāmātiō, from exclāmō (“to cry out”) + -tiō.

parole.significato: The act of offering an excuse or apology, or the fact of being excused; an excuse, a defence.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French excusation, from Latin excūsātiō, from excūsō (“to excuse”).

parole.significato: Designed or fitted for execution, or carrying into effect.
parole.testo: From Middle French executif, from Latin executivus, from Latin exsequi, from ex- ‘out’ + sequi ‘follow’.

parole.significato: Something fit to be imitated; an ideal, a worthy model or role model: a desirable example.
parole.testo: From Middle English exempler, from Middle French exemplair, and its source, Latin exemplar, from Latin exemplum (“example”).

parole.significato: Exemplary.
parole.testo: From Middle English exempler, from Middle French exemplaire, and its source, Latin exemplāris. By surface analysis, example + -ar. Doublet of exemplary.

parole.significato: Free from a duty, obligation, rule, law, etc.
parole.testo: From Middle French exempt, from Latin exemptus, past participle of eximō.

parole.significato: To expel air from the lungs through the nose or mouth by action of the diaphragm, to breathe out.
parole.testo: From Middle French exhaler, from Latin exhalare, from ex (“out”) + halare (“to breathe”).

parole.significato: A person, especially a priest or priestess, who is a practitioner in exorcism to force out evil spirits or demons from…
parole.testo: From Middle French exorciste, from Latin exorcista, from Ancient Greek ἐξορκιστής (exorkistḗs).

parole.significato: Foreign, especially in an exciting way.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French exotique, from Latin exōticus, from Ancient Greek ἐξωτικός (exōtikós, “foreign”, literally “from the outside”), from ἐξω- (exō-, “outside”), from ἐξ (ex, “out of”).

parole.significato: The act or state of expecting or looking forward to an event as about to happen.
parole.testo: From Middle French expectation, from Latin exspectātiō, from exspectō (“expect”). By surface analysis, expect + -ation. Displaced native Old English wēn.

parole.significato: A military journey; an enterprise against some enemy or into enemy territory.
parole.testo: From Middle French expédition, and its source, Latin expeditio.

parole.significato: An act of atonement for a sin or wrongdoing.
parole.testo: From Middle French expiation, from Latin expiātiō(n) (“satisfaction”).

parole.significato: To die.
parole.testo: From Middle English expire, from Middle French expirer, from Latin expīrō, exspīrō, from ex- (“out”) + spīrō (“breathe, be alive”).

parole.significato: Able to be explained.
parole.testo: From Middle French explicable, from Latin explicabilis, from explicō (“unfold, explain”).

parole.significato: The act of opening or unfolding.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French explication and its etymon Latin explicātiō, explicātiōnem. By surface analysis, explicate + -ion.

parole.significato: The process of exploring.
parole.testo: From Middle French exploration, from Latin exploratio. Morphologically explore + -ation.

parole.significato: Synonym of explorer.
parole.testo: From Middle English exploratour (“scout or spy”), from Middle French explorateur and its etymon Latin explōrātor.

parole.significato: To seek for something or after someone.
parole.testo: From Middle French explorer, from Latin explōrāre (“to investigate, search out”), itself said to be originally a hunters' term meaning "to set up a loud cry", from ex- (“out”) + plōrāre (“to cry”), but the second element is also explained as "to make to flow" (from pluere (“to flow”)). parole.significato: A person affiliated with an institution in a lesser capacity, for example, as a non-resident or as a part-time affiliat…
parole.testo: From Middle French externe or its etymon Latin externus.

parole.significato: Very cheery and peppy; extremely cheerful, energetic and enthusiastic.
parole.testo: From Middle French exubérant, from Latin exūberāns, the present active participle of exūberō (“be abundant”). Put together from ex (“out”), and uber (“udder”), and originally would have referred to a cow or she-goat which was making so much milk that it naturally dripped or sprayed from the udder.

parole.significato: To rejoice; to be very happy, especially in triumph; to triumph (over).
parole.testo: From Middle French exulter, from Latin exsultō, frequentative of exsiliō (“jump up”), from ex- + saliō (“jump, leap”).

parole.significato: The act of fabricating, framing, or constructing; construction; manufacture
parole.testo: From Middle French fabrication, from Latin fabricatio. Equivalent to fabricate + -ion.

parole.significato: Easy; contemptibly easy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French facile, from Latin facilis (“easy to do, easy, doable”), from Latin facere (“to do, make”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- (“to do, put”) Compare Spanish and Portuguese fácil (“easy”), Catalan fàcil, Romanian facil. parole.significato: A group of people, especially within a political organization, which expresses a shared belief or opinion different fro…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French faction, from Latin factiō (“a group of people acting together, a political faction”), noun of process from perfect passive participle factus, from faciō (“do, make”). Doublet of fashion.

parole.significato: The state of being extremely friendly; intimacy.
parole.testo: From Middle French familiarité, from Latin familiāritātem. Displaced native Old English hīwcūþnes. Morphologically familiar + -ity.

parole.significato: Extreme shortage of food in a region.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French famine, itself from the root of Latin fames.

parole.significato: A person who maintains the health and balance of horses' feet through the trimming of the hoofs and fitting of horsesho…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French ferrier, from Old French ferrier, from Latin ferrārius, from ferrum (“iron”).

parole.significato: Proceeding from, or appointed by, fate or destiny.
parole.testo: From Middle French fatal, from Latin fātālis (“fatal”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to feces.
parole.testo: From Middle French fecal, from Latin faex, equivalent to feces + -al.

parole.significato: Dirty with faeces or other impurities
parole.testo: From Middle French feculent, from Latin faeculentus, from faex.

parole.significato: Highly fertile; able to produce offspring.
parole.testo: From Middle French fécond, from Latin fēcundus (“fertile”), which is related to fētus and fēmina (“woman”).

parole.significato: To react, using fermentation; especially to produce alcohol by aging or by allowing yeast to act on sugars; to brew.
parole.testo: From Middle English ferment, from Middle French ferment, from Latin fermentāre (“to leaven, ferment”), from fermentum (“substance causing fermentation”), possibly from contraction of *fervimentum, from fervēre. See also fervent.

parole.significato: The condition of being ferocious.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French férocité, from Latin ferocitas, from ferox (“fierce”), from ferus (“wild, savage, fierce”).

parole.significato: Of land, etc.: capable of growing abundant crops; productive.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Middle French fertile, from Old French fertile, from Latin fertilis (“fruitful, fertile”), from ferō (“to bear, carry”).

parole.significato: The condition, or the degree, of being fertile.
parole.testo: From Middle French fertilité, from Latin fertilitās, equivalent to fertile + -ity.

parole.significato: A ruler-shaped instrument, generally used to slap naughty children on the hand.
parole.testo: From Middle French ferule (modern French férule), from Latin ferula (“giant fennel”). Doublet of ferula.

parole.significato: festive, relating to a festival or feast
parole.testo: From Middle French festal, from Latin festum (“feast”).

parole.significato: A festival or similar celebration.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English festivite, from Middle French festivité, from Latin festīvitas, equivalent to festive + -ity.

parole.significato: The killing of a fetus or embryo; an induced abortion.
parole.testo: From fetus + -cide or fetus + -icide, from Middle French -cide, from Latin -cīda (“cutter, killer”) and its derivation -cīdium (“killing”), from -cīd (combining form of caedō (“cut, kill”)) + -a (“-er”, forming agent nouns).

parole.significato: Land held in feudal tenure.
parole.testo: From Middle English feu, from Middle French fé (“fief”), fié, fief, fieu, from Latin feodum.

parole.significato: The act of giving figure or determinate form.
parole.testo: Late Middle English figuracion, from Middle French figuration, from Latin figūrō (“to form”). Equivalent to figurate + -ion.

parole.significato: A skill in the handling or manipulation of a situation.
parole.testo: From Middle English finesse (“a degree of excellence; (of metal) fineness, purity”), from Middle French finesse, Old French finesse (“a fineness; a delicacy; slenderness”), from fine, fin (“fine, thin”) (from Latin fīnis (“an end”); compare Middle English fīn (“of superior quality; precious, valuabl

parole.significato: The public treasury of Rome.
parole.testo: Partly from Middle French fisc and partly from its etymon, Latin fiscus (“basket, money-bag, public treasury”); see fiscal.

parole.significato: Related to the treasury of a country, company, region or city, particularly to government spending and revenue.
parole.testo: From Middle French fiscal, from Latin fiscus (“treasury”) – see fiscus and fisc.

parole.significato: Obvious and offensive; blatant; scandalous.
parole.testo: From Middle French flagrant, from Latin flagrantem, present participle of flagrare (“blaze, burn”). More at black.

parole.significato: Capable of being flexed or bent without breaking; able to be turned or twisted without breaking.
parole.testo: From Middle French flexible, from Latin flexibilis, from flectō (“to bend, curve”). Morphologically flex + -ible.

parole.significato: The leaves of plants.
parole.testo: From earlier foilage, from Late Middle English ffoylage, from Middle French feuillage. The more recent form is influenced by Latin folium (“leaf”).

parole.significato: Fortuitous.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French fortuit, from Latin fortuitus.

parole.significato: The iron worker in charge of the blast furnace and the smelting operation.
parole.testo: From Middle French fondeur, from Latin fundo (“pour, melt, cast”).

parole.significato: A severe laminitis of a horse, caused by untreated internal inflammation in the hooves.
parole.testo: From Middle French fondrer (“send to the bottom”), from Latin fundus (“bottom”).

parole.significato: A female founder (“one who founds or casts metals”).
parole.testo: From founder (“one who founds or casts metals”) + -ess (suffix forming female forms of words). Founder is derived from Middle French fondeur (“owner of a foundry; ironworker in charge of smelting, founder”) (modern French fondeur), from Latin fundātor (“founder”) (rare): see further at etymology 1.

parole.significato: Easily broken, not sturdy; of delicate material.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French fragile, from Latin fragilis, formed on frag-, the root of frangere (“to break”). Cognate with fraction, fracture and doublet of frail.

parole.significato: The condition or quality of being fragile; brittleness; frangibility.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French fragilité, from Latin fragilitās. Doublet of frailty. Morphologically fragile + -ity.

parole.significato: The killing of one's brother (or sister).
parole.testo: From Middle French fratricide or its etymon Latin frātricīdium.

parole.significato: A person who commits fratricide.
parole.testo: From Middle English fratricide, from Middle French fratricide or its etymon Latin frātricīda.

parole.significato: The rubbing of one object or surface against another.
parole.testo: From Middle French friction and directly from Latin frictionem, nom. frictio (“a rubbing, rubbing down”).

parole.significato: The state of being frigid; coldness; lack of heat.
parole.testo: From Middle English frigiditee, frigidite, a borrowing from Middle French frigidité, itself a borrowing from Latin frīgiditātem, accusative of Latin frīgiditās.

parole.significato: Careful or wise in expenditure; avoiding waste.
parole.testo: From Middle French, from Latin frugalis (“virtuous, thrifty”). Displaced native Old English spærhende (literally “spare-handed”).

parole.significato: The act of fulminating or exploding; detonation.
parole.testo: From Middle French fulmination, from Latin fulminātiō; equivalent to fulmine + -ation.

parole.significato: What something does or is used for.
parole.testo: From Middle French function, from Old French fonction, from Latin functiō (“performance, execution”), from functus, perfect participle of fungor (“to perform, execute, discharge”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewg- (“to enjoy”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to a funeral.
parole.testo: From Middle French funerail, from Latin funereus + -al.

parole.significato: A general uproar or commotion.
parole.testo: From Middle English furour, from Middle French fureur, from Old French furor, from Latin furor, from furō (“To rage, to be out of one's mind”).

parole.significato: Of a thing: done with evasive or guilty secrecy.
parole.testo: From Middle English *furtyve (implied in furtyvely (adverb)), from Middle French furtif, furtive (“furtive, stealthy”) (modern French furtif), from Latin fūrtīvus (“clandestine, furtive, secret; concealed, hidden; stolen”), from fūrtum (“theft; robbery”) (from fūr (“thief”), ultimately from Proto-In

parole.significato: A light flintlock musket or firelock.
parole.testo: From Middle French fusil, ultimately from Latin focus (“hearth; fire”). Doublet of fusee.

parole.significato: The act of merging separate things, or the result thereof.
parole.testo: First appears c. 1555, in a translation by Richard Eden. From Middle French fusion, from Latin fūsiōnem (the accusative of fūsiō), from fusus, past participle of fundō (“to pour; to melt”) (see also found). Doublet of foison.

parole.significato: Incapable of producing results, useless; doomed not to be successful; not worth attempting.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French futile, from Latin fūtilis.

parole.significato: To engender.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English gendren, from Middle French gendrer, from Latin generāre.

parole.significato: Very broad; pertaining or appropriate to large classes or groups as opposed to specific instances.
parole.testo: From Middle French générique, from Latin genus (“genus, kind”) + -ic.

parole.significato: Noble in behaviour or actions; principled, not petty; kind, magnanimous.
parole.testo: From Middle French genereux, and its source, Latin generōsus (“of noble birth”), from genus (“race, stock”).

parole.significato: Friendly and cheerful; enlivening.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French génial, borrowed from Latin geniālis (“of or pertaining to marriage; festive”), from genius (“guardian spirit”) + -ālis.

parole.significato: The study of the physical properties of the earth, including how humans affect and are affected by them.
parole.testo: From Middle French géographie, from Latin geōgraphia, from Ancient Greek γεωγραφία (geōgraphía, “a description of the earth”), from γῆ (gê, “earth”) + γράφω (gráphō, “write”). parole.significato: The small mass of cells from which a new organism develops; a seed, bud, spore, or zygote.
parole.testo: From Middle French germe, from Latin germen (“bud, seed, embryo”). Doublet of germen.

parole.significato: Any spherical (or nearly spherical) object.
parole.testo: From late Middle English globe, from Middle French globe, from Old French globe, borrowed from Latin globus. Doublet of globus.

parole.significato: The act of glorifying or the state of being glorified.
parole.testo: From Middle English glorificacion, glorificacioun, from Middle French glorification and its etymon Latin glōrificātiō. By surface analysis, glorify + -ication.

parole.significato: Fibrin (formerly considered as one of the "animal humours").
parole.testo: From Middle French gluten, borrowed from Latin glūten (“glue”).

parole.significato: That which steers a nautical vessel; a rudder or a person employing it.
parole.testo: From Middle English governail, governaile from Middle French and Old French governail, from Latin gubernāculum. Doublet of gubernaculum.

parole.significato: Lean, slender, thin.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French gracil, gracile (“slender, thin”) (modern French gracile (“gracile”)), or directly from its etymon Latin gracilis (“slender, slim, thin; lean, meagre, scanty; simple, unadorned”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kerḱ- (“to become thin; to wane”). The sense “graceful

parole.significato: graciousness, usually in a bad sense, as implying duplicity
parole.testo: From Middle English graciousete, partly from Middle French gracieuseté, partly modelled on Latin grātiōsitās, and probably also partly equivalent to gracious + -osity.

parole.significato: A rating.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French grade (“a grade, degree”), from Latin gradus (“a step, pace, degree”), from Proto-Italic *graðus, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰradʰ-, *gʰredʰ- (“to walk, go”). parole.significato: Not breaching any constraints of the grammar, or morpho-syntax, of the relevant language.
parole.testo: From Middle French grammatical, from Latin grammaticālis.

parole.significato: The state of being grand or splendid; magnificence.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French grandeur, from Old French grandur, from grant (French grand), from Latin grandis (“grown up, great”).

parole.significato: Lofty, pompous or bombastic speech or writing.
parole.testo: From Middle French grandiloquence, from Latin grandiloquentia, from grandiloquus, 1580s.

parole.significato: Given to using language in a showy way by using an excessive number of difficult words to impress others; bombastic; tu…
parole.testo: From Middle French grandiloquent, from Latin grandiloquus, from grandis (“great, full”) + loquēns, present participle of loquor (“to speak”). Compare eloquent.

parole.significato: Safe and comfortable, where humans, or other animals, can live; fit for habitation.
parole.testo: From Middle English abitable, habytable, from Middle French habitable, from Latin habitābilis (“habitable”), from habitō (“dwell, live”). By surface analysis, habit (“inhabit”) + able.

parole.significato: A dwelling or habitation.
parole.testo: From Middle English habitacle, from Middle French habitacle, from Latin habitāculum (“dwelling place”). See binnacle, habit (verb), inhabit.

parole.significato: The essential character of one's being or existence; native or normal constitution; mental or moral constitution; bodil…
parole.testo: From Middle English habitude, from Middle French habitude, from Latin habitūdō (“condition, plight, habit, appearance”), from habeō (“to have, hold, keep”).

parole.significato: A mythological creature generally depicted as a bird-of-prey with the head of a maiden, a face pale with hunger and lon…
parole.testo: Ultimately from Middle French harpie, from Latin harpyia, from Ancient Greek ἅρπυιᾰ (hárpuiă, literally “snatcher”), from ἁρπάζω (harpázō, “to snatch, seize”). Compare rapacious. Middle English had arpie.

parole.significato: A characteristic trait of the Hebrew language. By extension it is sometimes applied to the Jewish people or their faith…
parole.testo: From Middle French hebraisme or Latin Hebraismus; equivalent to Hebra- + -ism.

parole.significato: An iron ore, mainly peroxide of iron, Fe₂O₃: iron(III) oxide.
parole.testo: From Middle French hematite, from Latin (lapis) haematites, from Ancient Greek αἱματίτης (haimatítēs) λίθος (líthos, “blood-red stone”), from αἷμα (haîma, “blood”). By surface analysis, hemat- + -ite.

parole.significato: Hereditary transmission of the physical and genetic qualities of parents to their offspring; the biological law by whic…
parole.testo: From Middle French heredité, from Latin hērēditas (“condition of being an heir”), from hēres (“heir”).

parole.significato: Synonym of inherit.
parole.testo: From Middle English heriten, from Middle French heriter (modern French hériter), from Old French eriter, heriter, earlier *hereter, from Latin hērēditō.

parole.significato: Of or relating to a hero or heroine; supremely noble.
parole.testo: Partly from Middle French heroïque and partly from Latin hērōicus. By surface analysis, hero + -ic.

parole.significato: Synonym of historical or historic.
parole.testo: From Middle English historial, from Middle French historial (French historial) and its etymon Latin historiālis. By surface analysis, history + -al. Piecewise doublet of storial.

parole.significato: Any Old World bird of genus Upupa, especially Upupa epops (Eurasian hoopoe), known for its distinctive plumage, fanlike…
parole.testo: Alteration of obsolete hoopoop, from earlier hoop, from Middle French and Old French huppe, from Latin upupa, ultimately onomatopoeic; Compare Ancient Greek ἔποψ (épops), Persian پوپو (popo).

parole.significato: The visible horizontal line (in all directions) where the sky appears to meet the earth in the distance.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English orisonte, orisoun, from Middle French horizon, horizonte, from Old French orisonte, orison, via Latin horizōn, from Ancient Greek ὁρίζων (horízōn), from ὅρος (hóros, “boundary”).

parole.significato: Perpendicular to the vertical; parallel to the plane of the horizon; level, flat.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French horizontal, from horizon, horizonte, from Latin horizōn (stem horizont-).

parole.significato: Giving exhortation or advice; encouraging.
parole.testo: From Middle French hortatoire, from Latin hortor (“encourage”).

parole.significato: cordial and generous towards guests
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French hospitable, formed from the root of Latin hospitare with the suffix -able. Displaced native Old English cumlīþe (literally “guest-gentle”).

parole.significato: the consecrated bread or wafer of the Eucharist, host.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French hostie, from Latin hostia.

parole.significato: Not friendly; appropriate to an enemy; showing the disposition of an enemy; showing ill will and malevolence or a desir…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French hostile, from Latin hostīlis, from hostis (“enemy”). Displaced Old English fēondlīċ.

parole.significato: Of or belonging to the species Homo sapiens or its closest relatives.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English humaigne, humayne, humain, from Middle French humain, from Old French humain, umain (“of or belonging to man”, adjective), from Latin hūmānus m (“of man, human”, adjective); see there for further details. parole.significato: One who worships idols; (historical) a pagan.
parole.testo: From Middle English ydolatrer, from Middle French idolatre, from Latin idololatra. Displaced native Old English dēofolġielda (literally “devil worshiper”).

parole.significato: Not noble; plebeian; common.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French ignoble, from Latin ignōbilis, from in- (“not”) + gnōbilis, later nōbilis (“noble”).

parole.significato: Especially of a person: deserving of disgrace or dishonour; contemptible, despicable.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English ignominious (“disgraceful, shameful”), from Middle French ignominieux (modern French ignominieux), or from its etymon Latin ignōminiōsus (“disgraced; disgraceful, shameful, ignominious”), from ignōminia (“disgrace, dishonour, shame, ignominy”) + -ōsus (suffix meaning ‘full o

parole.significato: Restricting or failing to sufficiently promote individual choice and freedom.
parole.testo: From Middle French illibéral, from Latin illiberalis, equivalent to il- + liberal.

parole.significato: Resulting from an illusion; deceptive, imaginary, unreal.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French illusorie (modern French illusoire), derived from Latin illūsōrius (“mocking, ironical”).

parole.significato: The act of illustrating; the act of making clear and distinct.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French illustration, from Latin illūstrātiō, from illūstrō (“to illustrate”). By surface analysis, illustrate + -ion.

parole.significato: Synonym of illustrious.
parole.testo: From Middle French illustre (French illustre), from Latin illūstris (“bright, shining, brilliant, lustrous; clear, lucid; illustrious, distinguished, famous”), from illūstrō (“to illustrate”).

parole.significato: To illuminate (something).
parole.testo: From Middle English illustren, from Middle French illustrer (French illustrer), from Latin illūstrāre (“to illustrate”).

parole.significato: To form a mental image of something; to envision or create something in one's mind.
parole.testo: From Middle English ymagynen, from Middle French imaginer, from Latin imāginor, from imāginem, the accusative singular of imāgō (“a copy, likeness, image”).

parole.significato: A person with limited mental capacity who can perform tasks and think only like a young child, in medical circles meani…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French imbécile, from Latin imbēcillus (“weak, feeble”), literally “without a staff”.

parole.significato: The act of imitating.
parole.testo: From Middle English imitacioun, from Middle French imitacion, from Old French imitacion, from Latin imitatio.

parole.significato: Permanent, enduring; that does not perish.
parole.testo: From Middle French inmarcessible (1482), later immarcescible (“that does not shrivel" or "that does not perish”), from Latin immarcescibilis (“unfading”).

parole.significato: Incurable; not able to be assisted by medicine.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French immedicable and its source, Latin immedicābilis.

parole.significato: The act of immolating, or the state of being immolated.
parole.testo: From Middle English immolacion, from Middle French immolation, from Old French, from Latin immolatio.

parole.significato: Exempt; not subject to.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Middle French immun, from Latin immūnis (“exempt from public service”), from in- (“not”) + mūnus (“service”).

parole.significato: To cloister, confine, imprison or hole up: to lock someone up or seclude oneself behind walls.
parole.testo: From Middle English enmuren and Middle French emmurer, both from Old French enmurer, from Latin immūrō, from in- + mūrus (“wall”). Modern spelling is modelled after the Latin.

parole.significato: The state or quality of being immutable; immutableness.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French immutabilité, itself borrowed from Latin immūtābilitās. By surface analysis, immutable + -ity.

parole.significato: Perfect, without faults, flaws or errors
parole.testo: From Middle French impeccable, from Latin impeccabilis (“not liable to sin”), from im- (“not”) + peccare (“to err, to sin”).

parole.significato: Not penetrable.
parole.testo: From Middle English inpenetrabel, inpenetrabyle, from Middle French impenetrable or directly from its etymon, Latin impenetrābilis. By surface analysis, im- + penetrable.

parole.significato: Insolent, ill-mannered or disrespectful; Disregardful.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English impertinent, from Middle French impertinent, from Old French impertinent, from Latin impertinēns; by surface analysis, im- + pertinent.

parole.significato: To fix firmly or set securely or deeply.
parole.testo: From Middle French implanter, from Latin implantō. By surface analysis, im- + plant.

parole.significato: The act of implicating.
parole.testo: From Middle French implication, from Latin implicationem (accusative of implicatio). Equivalent to implicate + -ion.

parole.significato: Suggested indirectly, without being directly expressed; Implied.
parole.testo: From Middle French implicite, from Latin implicitus, past participle of implico (“to infold, involve, entangle”); see implicate.

parole.significato: Something that is impossible.
parole.testo: From Middle French impossibilité, from Latin impossibilitās. By surface analysis, im- + possibility and impossible + -ity.

parole.significato: A tax, tariff or duty that is imposed, especially on merchandise.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French impost, itself borrowed or adapted from Latin impōsitus, past participle of impōnō (“to impose”).

parole.significato: Someone who attempts to deceive by using an assumed name or identity.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French imposteur, respelled in the Latin manner; ultimately from Latin impositor, agent form of Latin imponere (“to impose”).

parole.significato: Powerlessness; incapacity.
parole.testo: From Middle French impotence, from Latin impotentia.

parole.significato: Unsuitable to needs or circumstances; inappropriate; inapt.
parole.testo: From Middle French impropre, from Latin improprius (“not proper”), from in- + proprius (“proper”). By surface analysis, im- + proper.

parole.significato: The quality or state of being imprudent; lack of prudence, caution, discretion or circumspection.
parole.testo: From im- + prudence. From Middle French imprudence, from Latin imprudentia.

parole.significato: Not prudent; lacking prudence or discretion; indiscreet; injudicious; not paying attention to the consequences of one's…
parole.testo: From Middle French imprudent, from Latin imprūdens (“not foreseeing, ignorant”), prefix im- (“not”) + prūdens (“foreseeing, skilled, judicious”).

parole.significato: The quality of being impudent, not showing due respect.
parole.testo: From Middle French impudence, from Latin impudentia.

parole.significato: Immodesty; shamelessness.
parole.testo: From Middle French impudicité, from Latin impudicus (“shameless, immodest”) + Middle French -ité. By surface analysis, im- + pudic + -ity.

parole.significato: To assault, attack.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French impugner, from Latin impugnō, from im- + pugnō (“fight”), from pugnus (“fist”), as in English pugilism (“fighting with fists, boxing”).

parole.significato: A thrust; a push; a sudden force that impels.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French impulser, from Latin impulsus.

parole.significato: Having the power of driving or impelling; giving an impulse; moving; impellent.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French impulsif, from Latin impulsivus.

parole.significato: Exemption from punishment.
parole.testo: From Middle French impunité, from Latin impunitas, from impunis (“without punishment”).

parole.significato: Not pure
parole.testo: From Middle French impur, from Latin impūrus.

parole.significato: The condition of being impure; because of contamination, pollution, adulteration or insufficient purification.
parole.testo: From impure + -ity. From Middle French impurité, from Latin impuritas.

parole.significato: The act of imputing or charging; attribution; ascription.
parole.testo: From Middle French imputation, from Latin imputatio.

parole.significato: To attribute or ascribe (responsibility or fault) to a cause or source.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French imputer, from Latin imputō (“to bring into the reckoning, charge, impute”).

parole.significato: The quality or state of being inaccessible; inaccessibleness.
parole.testo: From Middle French inaccessibilité, from Latin inaccessibilitas.

parole.significato: Not certain, uncertain.
parole.testo: From Middle English incertayne, borrowed from Middle French incertain, derived in the 14th c. from certain, after Latin incertus (“uncertain”). By surface analysis, in- + certain.

parole.significato: An event or occurrence.
parole.testo: Recorded since 1412, from Middle French incident, from Latin incidens, the present active participle of incidō (“to happen, befall”), itself from in- (“on”) + -cidō, the combining form of cadō (“to fall”).

parole.significato: To call into action.
parole.testo: From Middle French inciter, from Latin incitō (“to set in motion, hasten, urge, incite”), from in (“in, on”) + citō (“to set in motion, urge”), frequentative of cieō (“to rouse, excite, call”).

parole.significato: Not comparable.
parole.testo: From Middle English incomparable, from Middle French incomparable, from Old French [Term?], from Latin incomparābilis. By surface analysis, in- + comparable.

parole.significato: Impossible or very difficult to understand.
parole.testo: From Middle French incomprehensible, from Latin incomprehēnsibilis. Equivalent to in- + comprehensible.

parole.significato: Lack of due consideration; inattention to consequences, thoughtlessness.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French inconsideration and its source, Latin incōnsiderātiōnem.

parole.significato: Not consolable; unable to be consoled or comforted, usually due to grief, disappointment, or other distress.
parole.testo: Middle French inconsolable, from Latin inconsolabilis; by surface analysis, in- + consolable, or, by surface analysis, in- + console + -able.

parole.significato: Not constant; wavering.
parole.testo: From Middle English inconstant, inconstante, inconstaunte, from Middle French inconstant and its etymon, Latin incōnstāns.

parole.significato: not convenient
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French inconvenient, from Latin inconvenientem.

parole.significato: Defective and impossible to materially correct or set aright.
parole.testo: From Middle English incorrigible, from Middle French incorrigible (1334), or directly from Latin incorrigibilis (“not to be corrected”), from in- (“not”) + corrigere (“to correct”) + -ibilis (“-able”), equivalent to in- + corrigible. Recorded since 1340.

parole.significato: Incapable of being bribed or morally corrupted; inflexibly just and upright.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French incorruptible, from Latin incorruptibilis. By surface analysis, in- + corruptible.

parole.significato: Extremely persistent and untiring.
parole.testo: From Middle French, from Latin indēfatīgābilis (“untiring”), from in- (“not”) + dēfatīgō (“to tire out”).

parole.significato: Without loss or injury.
parole.testo: From Middle French indemne and indempne, from Latin indemnis (“unhurt”), from in- (“not”) + damnum (“hurt, damage; wrong”). Compare damn and condemn.

parole.significato: Indigenous.
parole.testo: From Middle French indigène, from Latin indigena.

parole.significato: Unworthy, undeserving.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French indigne, from Latin indignus, from in- (“un-”) + dignus (“worthy, dignified”).

parole.significato: Lasting; indestructible; not possible to dissolve, disintegrate or break up.
parole.testo: From Middle French indissoluble, from Latin indissolubilis.

parole.significato: not clearly defined or not having a sharp outline; faint or dim
parole.testo: From Middle French indistinct, from Latin indistinctus. English equivalent in- + distinct.

parole.significato: The act of indulging.
parole.testo: From Middle English indulgence, indulgens, from Middle French indulgence and its source, Latin indulgentia.

parole.significato: Beyond expression in words; unspeakable.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French ineffable, a learned borrowing from Latin ineffābilis, from in- (“not”) + effābilis (“utterable”).

parole.significato: Not elegant; not exhibiting neatness, refinement, or precision.
parole.testo: From Middle French inélégant, from Latin inēlegāns; equivalent to in- + elegant.

parole.significato: Impossible to avoid or escape; inescapable, irresistible.
parole.testo: From Middle French inéluctable (whence in- + e- and -able), from Latin inēlūctābilis, from in- + ēlūctor (“struggle out”) + -bilis.

parole.significato: Not able to do something; not proficient; displaying incompetence.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French inepte, from Latin ineptus, from in- + aptus (whence English apt).

parole.significato: Not able to be estimated; not able to be calculated, computed or comprehended, as because of great scale, degree or mag…
parole.testo: From Middle French inestimable, from Latin inaestimābilis, from in (“un-”, “not”) + aestimābilis (“estimable”). Equivalent to in- + estimable.

parole.significato: Impossible to avoid or prevent.
parole.testo: From Middle French inevitable, from Latin inēvītābilis (“unavoidable”), from in- + ēvītābilis (“avoidable”), from ēvītāre (“to avoid”), from ē- (“out”) + vītāre (“to shun”).

parole.significato: not excusable
parole.testo: From Middle French inexcusable, from Latin inexcusabilis.

parole.significato: Impossible to prevent or stop; inevitable.
parole.testo: From Middle French inexorable, from Latin inexōrābilis (“relentless, inexorable”) (or directly from the Latin word), from in- (prefix meaning ‘not’) + exōrābilis (“that may be moved or persuaded by entreaty; exorable”). parole.significato: Inept or unskilled; not of expert ability or quality.
parole.testo: From Middle English inexpert, inexperte, from in- (“not”) + expert, experte, or else from Middle French inexpert or its etymon Latin inexpertus. By surface analysis, in- (“not”) + expert.

parole.significato: Impossible to explain; not easily accounted for.
parole.testo: From Middle English inexplicable, from Middle French inexplicable, from Latin inexplicābilis, from in- (“not”) + explicābilis (“explicable”). By surface analysis, in- + explicable.

parole.significato: Inextinguishable.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French inextinguible and its source, Latin inextinguibilis.

parole.significato: Impossible to untie or disentangle.
parole.testo: From Middle French inextricable, from Latin inextricabilis.

parole.significato: indefatigable
parole.testo: From Middle French infatigable, from Latin infatigabilis.

parole.significato: To bring (the body or part of it) into contact with a substance that causes illness (a pathogen), so that the pathogen…
parole.testo: From Middle French infect, from Latin infectus, perfect passive participle of inficiō (“dye, taint”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to hell, or the world of the dead; hellish.
parole.testo: From Middle French infernal, from Medieval Latin infernalis, from Latin īnfernus, from īnferum (“netherworld, underworld, hell”), equivalent to inferno + -al.

parole.significato: Rejecting a specific religion.
parole.testo: First attested 1460, from Middle French infidèle, from Latin īnfidēlis (“unfaithful”), from in- (“not”) + fidēlis (“faithful”). See fidelity.

parole.significato: Unfaithfulness in a marriage or an intimate (sexual or romantic) relationship: practice or instance of having a sexual…
parole.testo: From Middle English infidelite, from Middle French infidelité (modern French infidélité) and its etymon Latin īnfidēlitās. Equivalent to infidel + -ity.

parole.significato: The act of inflaming, kindling, or setting on fire.
parole.testo: From Middle French inflammation, from Latin īnflammātiō, equivalent to inflame + -ation.

parole.significato: The linguistic phenomenon of morphological variation, whereby words take a number of distinct forms in order to express…
parole.testo: From older inflexion, borrowed from Middle French inflexion, itself borrowed from Latin inflexiōnem (“alteration”, literally “bending”). The English spelling with ⟨ct⟩ is due to influence from inflect or related words like correction.

parole.significato: Not flexible; not capable of bending or being bent.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French inflexible, from Latin īnflexibilis. See also in- + flexible.

parole.significato: Dated spelling of inflection.
parole.testo: From Middle French inflexion, itself from Latin īnflexiō.

parole.significato: A minor offence, petty crime.
parole.testo: From Middle French infraction, from Latin infractio, from infractum, past participle of infringere, from in (“in”) + frangere (“to break”).

parole.significato: Of a person, displaying genius, ingenuity or brilliance; inventive.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French ingénieux, from Old French engenious, from Latin ingeniōsus (“endowed with good natural capacity, gifted with genius”), from ingenium (“innate or natural quality, natural capacity, genius”), from in- (“in”) + gignere (“to produce”), Old Latin genere. See also engine.

parole.significato: One of the substances present in a mixture, especially food.
parole.testo: From Middle French ingredient, from Latin ingrediens, present participle of ingredior (“to go or enter into or onto”).

parole.significato: Not habitable; not suitable to be inhabited.
parole.testo: From Middle English inhabitable, inhabytabill, from Middle French inhabitable and its etymon Latin inhabitābilis (“uninhabitable”). By surface analysis, in- + habitable.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to inhumanity and the indifferently cruel, sadistic or barbaric behavior it brings.
parole.testo: From Middle English inhumayne, from Middle French inhumain and its etymon Latin inhūmānus.

parole.significato: The lack of compassion.
parole.testo: From Middle French inhumanité, from Latin inhumanitas, equivalent to inhuman + -ity.

parole.significato: Beyond imitation, surpassing all others; matchless.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French inimitable, from Latin inimitabilis, corresponding to in- + imitable.

parole.significato: The act of initiating, or the process of being initiated or introduced.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French initiation, from Latin initiātiō. Morphologically initiate + -ion.

parole.significato: The act of injecting, or something that is injected.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French injection, from Latin iniectio. The mathematical sense is from French injection, introduced by Nicolas Bourbaki in their treatise Éléments de mathématique. Equivalent to inject + -ion.

parole.significato: disturbance
parole.testo: From Middle English inquietacion, inquietacioun, inquietacyon, inquietation, from Middle French inquietation and its etymon, Latin inquiētātiō.

parole.significato: An arthropod (in the Insecta class) characterized by six legs, up to four wings, and a chitinous exoskeleton.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French insecte, from Latin īnsectum, from īnsectus (“cut into, cut up, with a notched or divided body”), from perfect passive participle of īnsecō (“to cut into, to cut up”), from in- + secō (“to cut”), from the notion that the insect's body is "cut into" three sections (head, t

parole.significato: Unable to be separated; bound together permanently.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Middle French inséparable, from Latin īnsēparābilis. Constructed as in- + separable.

parole.significato: Causing harm in a stealthy, often gradual, manner.
parole.testo: From Middle French insidieux, from Latin īnsidiōsus (“cunning, artful, deceitful”), from īnsidiae (“a lying in wait, an ambush, artifice, stratagem”) + -ōsus, from īnsideō (“to sit in or on”), from in (“in, on”) + sedeō (“to sit”).

parole.significato: The act or process of insinuating; a creeping, winding, or flowing in.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French insinuation, from Old French, from Latin insinuatio, from īnsinuō (“to push in, creep in, steal in”), from in (“in”) + sinus (“a winding, bend, bay, fold, bosom”).

parole.significato: To hold up a claim emphatically.
parole.testo: Partly from Middle French insister, from Latin īnsistere; and partly from a back-formation from insistence. Compare typologically from the same PIE root Bulgarian настоявам (nastojavam), Russian наста́ивать (nastáivatʹ).

parole.significato: Contemptible, ill-mannered conduct; insulting: arrogant, bold behaviour or attitude.
parole.testo: From Middle French insolence, from Latin īnsolentia.

parole.significato: That cannot be dissolved.
parole.testo: From Middle English insolible, from Middle French insoluble, from Latin insolūbilis, from in- + solūbilis. Piecewise doublet of insolvable and unsolvable. By surface analysis, in- + soluble.

parole.significato: The act of examining something, often closely.
parole.testo: From Middle French, from Old French inspeccion, from Latin īnspectiō (“examination, inspection”), from the verb īnspiciō (“to inspect”), from speciō (“to look at”). By surface analysis, inspect + -ion.

parole.significato: The quality of being unstable.
parole.testo: From Middle French instabilité, from Latin instabilitas. Morphologically in- + stability.

parole.significato: Urgency of manner or words; an urgent request; insistence.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French instance, from Latin īnstantia (“a being near, presence, also perseverance, earnestness, importunity, urgency”), from īnstāns (“urgent”); see instant.

parole.significato: The act of instilling.
parole.testo: From Middle French instillation, from Latin instillatio.

parole.significato: Lacking substance; not real or strong.
parole.testo: Probably from Middle French insubstantiel, from Latin insubstantiālis, from in- + substantiālis. By surface analysis, in- + substantial.

parole.significato: An inadequate quantity of; not enough.
parole.testo: From Middle French insufficient, from Latin insufficiens. See also in- + sufficient.

parole.significato: To be insensitive, insolent, or rude to (somebody); to affront or demean (someone).
parole.testo: The verb is derived from Middle French insulter (modern French insulter (“to insult”)) or its etymon Latin īnsultō (“to spring, leap or jump at or upon; to abuse, insult, revile, taunt”), the frequentative form of īnsiliō (“to bound; to leap in or upon”), from in- (prefix meaning ‘in, inside, within

parole.significato: The action of part or all of a national population violently rising up against the government or other authority; (coun…
parole.testo: From Late Middle English insurreccion (“uprising against a government, rebellion, revolt; civil disorder, riot; illegal armed assault”) [and other forms], from Middle French insurrection, Old French insurreccïon (modern French insurrection), and from their etymon Latin īnsurrēctiōnem (rare), the acc

parole.significato: Left complete or whole; not touched, defiled, sullied, or otherwise damaged.
parole.testo: From Middle French intact, from Latin intact(us).

parole.significato: That is part of a whole; integral
parole.testo: From Middle French intégrant, from Latin integrans.

parole.significato: Steadfast adherence to a strict moral or ethical code.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French intégrité, from Latin integritās (“soundness, integrity”), from integer. Doublet of entirety.

parole.significato: Of, related to, or caused by the intellect.
parole.testo: From Middle French intellectif and its etymon the post-Classical Latin intellēctīvus, from intellegō.

parole.significato: Of high or especially quick cognitive capacity, bright.
parole.testo: From Middle French intelligent, from Latin intellegēns (“discerning”), present active participle of intellegō (“understand, comprehend”), itself from inter (“between”) + legō (“choose, pick out, read”).

parole.significato: Capable of being understood; clear to the mind.
parole.testo: From Middle French intelligible, from Old French, from Latin intelligibilis.

parole.significato: Lack of moderation or temperance; excess.
parole.testo: From Middle French intempérance, from Latin intemperantia.

parole.significato: A course of action that a person intends to follow.
parole.testo: From Middle English entencioun, intention, from Old French entencion, from Latin intentiō, intentiōnem. Compare intent. Equivalent to intent + -ion.

parole.significato: To plead on someone else's behalf.
parole.testo: First attested in c. 1570. From Middle French intercéder, from Latin intercēdō, from inter- (“between”) + cēdō (“I go”) (English cede), literally “to (act as) go-between”.

parole.significato: The act of intervening or mediating between two parties.
parole.testo: First attested in the early 15th Century. From Middle French intercession, from Old French intercession, from Latin intercessiō, from intercēdō, from inter- (“between”) + cēdō (“to go”) (English cede), literally “go-between”.

parole.significato: Stopping and starting, occurring, or presenting at intervals; coming after a particular time span.
parole.testo: From Middle French intermittent, from Latin intermittens (“sending between”), from prefix inter- (“among, on”) + mittens (“sending”), from mittere (“to send”).

parole.significato: The act of interpellating (questioning); the period in which government officials are questioned about and explain an a…
parole.testo: From Middle French interpellation, from Latin interpellātiō; equivalent to interpellate + -ion or interpel + -ation.

parole.significato: To insert something (or oneself) between other things.
parole.testo: From Middle French interposer, influenced by poser (“to place, put”), from Latin interpōnō, from inter (“between”) + pōnō (“to place, put”).

parole.significato: The junction of two (or more) paths, streets, highways, or other thoroughfares.
parole.testo: From Middle French intersection and its etymon Latin intersectiō. By surface analysis, intersect + -ion.

parole.significato: The action of intervening; interfering in some course of events.
parole.testo: From Middle French intervention, from Latin interventiō. Morphologically intervene + -tion.

parole.significato: A hint; an indirect suggestion.
parole.testo: From Middle French intimation, from Latin intimatio. By surface analysis, intimate + -ion.

parole.significato: Not tolerable; not capable of being borne or endured.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English intolerable, borrowed from Middle French intolerable, from Latin intolerābilis. By surface analysis, in- + tolerable.

parole.significato: Intricate, entangled.
parole.testo: From Middle French intrincable, from Latin intrīcō (“to entangle”).

parole.significato: Innate, inherent, inseparable from the thing itself, essential.
parole.testo: From Middle French intrinsèque, from Latin intrīnsecus (“on the inside, inwardly”), from *intrim, an assumed adverbial form of inter (“within”) + secus (“by, on the side”).

parole.significato: useless; unprofitable.
parole.testo: From Middle French inutile, from Latin inutilis. Philippine usage is likely from Tagalog inutil, from Spanish inútil, from the same source. By surface analysis, in- + utile.

parole.significato: Any person with a disability or illness.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French invalide, from Latin invalidus (“infirm, weak”), from in- (“not”) + validus (“strong”).

parole.significato: The quality or state of being invincible; invincibleness.
parole.testo: From Middle French invincibilité, from Latin invincibilitas.

parole.significato: Impossible to defeat, destroy, or kill; too powerful to be defeated or overcome.
parole.testo: From Middle French invincible, from Latin invincibilis (“unconquerable”), from in- (“not”) + vincibilis (“conquerable”), from vincere (“to conquer”).

parole.significato: The quality or state of being inviolable; inviolableness.
parole.testo: From Middle French inviolabilité, from Latin inviolabilitas.

parole.significato: Not violable; not to be infringed.
parole.testo: From Middle French inviolable, from Latin inviolābilis (“untouchable”), from violō (“violate”). Equivalent to in- + violable. Piecewise doublet of unviolable.

parole.significato: The state of being invisible.
parole.testo: From Middle French invisibilité, from Latin invisibilitas.

parole.significato: To ask for the presence or participation of someone or something.
parole.testo: From Middle French inviter, from Latin invītō. Displaced native English lathe.

parole.significato: Incapable of being injured; not vulnerable.
parole.testo: From Middle French invulnérable, from Latin invulnerābilis, from vulnerābilis, from vulnerō (“to wound”), from vulnus (“wound”), equivalent to in- + vulnerable.

parole.significato: The quality of a statement that, when taken in context, may actually mean something different from, or the opposite of,…
parole.testo: First attested in 1502. From Middle French ironie, from Old French, from Latin īrōnīa, from Ancient Greek εἰρωνεία (eirōneía, “irony, pretext”), from εἴρων (eírōn, “one who feigns ignorance”).

parole.significato: An act of irradiating, or state of being irradiated.
parole.testo: From Middle French irradiacion, from Latin irradiatio. Morphologically irradiate + -ion.

parole.significato: Incapable of being repaired, amended, cured or rectified; unrepairable.
parole.testo: From Middle French irréparable, from Old French, from Latin irreparabilis, equivalent to ir- + reparable.

parole.significato: Unable to be retracted or reversed; final.
parole.testo: From Middle French irrévocable, from Latin irrevocabilis; equivalent to ir- + revoke + -able.

parole.significato: The act or process of irrigating, or the state of being irrigated; especially, the operation of causing water to flow o…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French irrigation, from Latin irrigatio.

parole.significato: The act of irritating or annoying.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French irritation, from Latin irrītātiō, from irrītāre (“to excite”). By surface analysis, irritate + -ion.

parole.significato: The action of irrupting or breaking into; a violent entry or invasion; an inbreaking; an intrusion.
parole.testo: From Middle French irruption, from Latin irruptiō(n).

parole.significato: A morbid condition, characterized by yellowness of the eyes, skin, and urine.
parole.testo: From Middle English jaundis, jaunis, from Middle French jaunisse, from jaune (“yellow”) + -isse (“-ness”). Jaune, from Old French jalne, from Latin galbinus (“yellowish”), from galbus (“yellow”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to the Jews, their culture or their religion.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French judaique (modern French judaïque) and its etymon Latin iūdaicus, from Ancient Greek Ἰουδαϊκός (Ioudaïkós), ultimately from Hebrew יְהוּדָה (y'hudá, “Judah”). By surface analysis, Juda + -ic.

parole.significato: Liable to slip, err, fall, or apostatize.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French labile, borrowed from Latin lābilis (“slipping, transitent”).

parole.significato: A thin layer or plate of material, as in certain kinds of armor.
parole.testo: From Middle French lame, from Latin lāmina. Doublet of lamina.

parole.significato: An expression of grief, suffering, sadness or regret.
parole.testo: A back-formation from lamentation or else from Middle French lamenter and its etymon Latin lāmentor (“to wail, weep”), from lāmentum (“wailing, moaning, weeping”); with formative -mentum, from the root *la-, probably ultimately imitative. Also see latrare.

parole.significato: Causing sorrow, distress or regret; deplorable, pitiful or distressing.
parole.testo: From Middle English lamentable, from Middle French lamentable, from Latin lāmentābilis (“full of sorrow, mournful; deplorable”), from lāmentor (“lament”), from lāmenta (“wailing, weeping”). By surface analysis, lament + -able.

parole.significato: The act of lamenting.
parole.testo: Recorded since 1375, from Middle English lamentacioun, from Middle French lamentation and its etymon Latin lāmentātiō (“wailing, moaning, weeping”), from the deponent verb lāmentor, from lāmentum (“wail; wailing”), itself from a Proto-Indo-European *leh₂- (“to howl”), presumed ultimately imitative.

parole.significato: The lanner falcon, Falco biarmicus.
parole.testo: From Middle French lanier (“cowardly”), possibly from Latin lānārius.

parole.significato: A temporary failure; a slip.
parole.testo: From Middle French laps, from Latin lāpsus, from lābī (“to slip”). Doublet of lapsus.

parole.significato: Having the effect of moving the bowels, or aiding digestion and preventing constipation.
parole.testo: From Middle French laxatif, from Latin laxātīvus (literally “relaxing, loosening”).

parole.significato: The state of being lax; looseness, lack of tension.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French laxité, itself borrowed from Latin laxitas, laxitatem, from laxus. By surface analysis, lax + -ity.

parole.significato: Lax; not strict; tolerant of dissent or deviation.
parole.testo: From Middle French lénient, from Latin lēniēns (whence -i- + -ent), present participle of lēnīre (“to soften, soothe”), from lēnis (“soft”).

parole.significato: leniency, mercy, forgiveness
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French lénité, from Latin lēnitās (whence -ity), from lēnis (“soft”).

parole.significato: The act of liberating or the state of being liberated.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French libération, and from Latin liberatio, liberationem (“a freeing”), from liberare past participle liberatus (“set free”); see liberate. By surface analysis, liberate + -ion.

parole.significato: tendon
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French lien, from Latin ligāmen (“bond”), from ligō (“tie, bind”).

parole.significato: A place or stead.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French lieu, from Old French leu, from Latin locum, accusative of locus (“place”). Doublet of locus. Attested earlier and in Middle English only as part of the partially calqued phrase in lieu of.

parole.significato: Any distinctive shape or line, etc.
parole.testo: From Middle French linéament, from Latin lineamentum, from linea (“line”).

parole.significato: A predetermined or prescribed set of rituals that are performed, usually by a religion; a book in which they are record…
parole.testo: From Middle French liturgie, from Latin liturgia, from Ancient Greek λειτουργία (leitourgía), from λειτ- (leit-), from λαός (laós, “people”) + -ουργός (-ourgós), from ἔργον (érgon, “work”) (the public work of the people done on behalf of the people).

parole.significato: Having a dark, bluish appearance.
parole.testo: From Middle English livid, livide, from Old French livide, from Latin līvidus (“bluish, livid; envious”), from līveō (“be of a bluish color or livid; envy”), from Proto-Italic *sliwēō, from Proto-Indo-European *sliwo-, suffixed form of *(s)leh₃y- (“bluish”). See also Old English slā (“sloe”), Welsh

parole.significato: Talkativeness; the quality of being loquacious.
parole.testo: From Middle French loquacité, from Latin loquācitās (whence -acity), from loquor (“to say, speak, tell, talk, utter”).

parole.significato: Having or demonstrating undivided and constant support for someone or something.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French loyal, from Old French loial, leial, leal, from Latin lēgālis. Doublet of legal and leal.

parole.significato: Emitting light; glowing brightly; shining.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French lumineus, from Latin lūminōsus.

parole.significato: A clever scheme or artful plot, usually crafted for evil purposes.
parole.testo: From Middle English machynacion, machynacyon, from Middle French machination and directly Latin māchinātiōnem, from māchinor (“devise, invent”). By surface analysis, machinate + -ion or machine + -ation.

parole.significato: A device that directs and controls energy, often in the form of movement or electricity, to produce a certain effect.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French machine, from Latin māchina (“a machine, engine, contrivance, device, stratagem, trick”), from Doric Greek μᾱχᾰνᾱ́ (mākhănā́), cognate with Attic Greek μηχᾰνή (mēkhănḗ, “a machine, engine, contrivance, device”), from which comes mechanical. Displaced native Old English se

parole.significato: To make wet or moist.
parole.testo: From Middle French madéfier, borrowed from Latin madefaciō.

parole.significato: A generous benefactor; specifically, a patron of literature or art.
parole.testo: Derived from Middle French mecenas, and its source, Latin Maecēnās (“literary patron”), from the name of Gaius Maecenas (c. 70–8 BCE), Roman statesman and patron of Horace and Virgil.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or befitting a master; authoritative.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French magistral, from Latin magistrālis, from magister (“master, teacher”) + -ālis. Doublet of mistral.

parole.significato: The quality of being magnanimous; kindness of nature; generosity.
parole.testo: From Middle French magnanimité, from Old French [Term?], from Latin magnanimitās.

parole.significato: Magnificent, splendid; illustrious.
parole.testo: From Middle French magnifique, and its source, Latin magnificus. Doublet of magnifico.

parole.significato: Grand, elegant or splendid in appearance.
parole.testo: From Middle English magnificent, from Middle French magnificent, from Latin magnificentior, comparative of magnificus (“great in deeds or sentiment, noble, splendid, etc.”), from magnus (“great”) + -ficēns, a form of -ficiēns, the regular form, in compounds, of faciēns, a participle of facere (“to d

parole.significato: To praise, glorify (someone or something, especially God).
parole.testo: From Middle English magnifien, from Middle French magnifier, from Latin magnificāre, from magnificus.

parole.significato: A bright green mineral, a basic copper carbonate, Cu₂CO₃(OH)₂; one of the principal ores of copper.
parole.testo: From Middle French malachite, from Latin molochītis, from Ancient Greek μολόχη (molókhē, “[leaf of the ... ] mallow plant”).

parole.significato: A curse.
parole.testo: From late Middle English malediccion, from Middle French malédiction, from Latin maledictiō (“curse”) from malus (“evil”) + dictiō (“speech”) noun of action from perfect passive participle dictus (“spoken”), from verb dīcō (“speak”).

parole.significato: Hostile attitude or feeling.
parole.testo: From Middle French malevolence, from Latin malevolentia (“malevolence”), derived from malevolēns (“malevolent”).

parole.significato: The quality of being malign or malignant; badness, evilness, monstrosity, depravity, maliciousness.
parole.testo: From Middle English malignete, malignitee, malignyte, malyngnite, from Middle French maligneté, from Latin malignitās. By surface analysis, malign + -ity. * (a group of goblins): Coined by David Malki in the 30 October 2009 Wondermark webcomic strip “Supernatural Collective Nouns”.

parole.significato: Nipple, breast.
parole.testo: From mammill(ary) + -o-, from Middle French mamillaire or directly from Latin mammillāris, from mamilla + -aris, diminutive of mamma.

parole.significato: manageable
parole.testo: From Middle English manyable, from Middle French maniable, from manier (“to manage”), from Latin manus (“hand”). By surface analysis, man(us) + -i- + -able.

parole.significato: A division of the Roman army numbering 120 (or sometimes 60) soldiers exclusive of officers; (generally, obsolete) any…
parole.testo: From Late Middle English maniple, manyple (“scarf worn as vestment, maniple”), borrowed from Middle French, Old French maniple, manipule (“handful; troop of soldiers; scarf worn as vestment”) (modern French manipule), from Latin manipulus (“bundle, handful; troop of soldiers”), from manus (“hand”) (

parole.significato: Gentleness, tameness.
parole.testo: Via Middle French mansuetude or directly from Latin mansuētūdō, from mansuētus, perfect passive participle of mansuēscō (“to tame”), from manus (“hand”) + suēscō (“become accustomed”).

parole.significato: Belonging to or characteristic of the sea; existing or found in the sea; formed or produced by the sea.
parole.testo: Recorded since c.1420 as Middle English marin, borrowed from Middle French marin, from Old French, from Latin marinus (“of the sea”), itself from mare (“sea”), from Proto-Indo-European *móri (“body of water, lake”) (cognate with Old English mere (“sea, lake, pool, pond”), Dutch meer, German Meer, al

parole.significato: Pertaining to marriage.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French marital, and its source, Latin marītālis, from marītus (“husband”).

parole.significato: Relating to or connected with the sea or its uses (as navigation, commerce, etc.).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French maritime, from Latin maritimus.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or suggestive of war; warlike.

parole.significato: An expert on mathematics; someone who studies mathematics.

parole.significato: morning

parole.significato: The process of becoming mature.

parole.significato: Fully developed; grown up in terms of physical appearance, behaviour or thinking; ripe.

parole.significato: To proceed toward maturity: full development or completion (either of concrete or of abstract things, e.g. plans, judgm…

parole.significato: A central vein or nerve, especially the median vein or median nerve running through the forearm and arm.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French median, from Latin mediānus (“of or pertaining to the middle”, adjective), from medius (“middle”) (see medium), from Proto-Indo-European *médʰyos (“middle”). Doublet of mean and mizzen. Cognate with Old English midde, middel (“middle”). More at middle.

parole.significato: One who negotiates between parties seeking mutual agreement.
parole.testo: From Middle English mediatour, mediatoure, mediatur, medyatour, from Middle French mediateur, mediatur or its etymon Latin mediātor (“one who mediates”), from mediātum, supine of mediō (“be in the middle”), from medius (“middle”). By surface analysis, mediate + -or.

parole.significato: A medicine, or all the medicines regularly taken by a patient.
parole.testo: From Middle English medicacioun, from Middle French médication and its etymon Latin medicātiō, from medicārī (“to heal, cure”), from medicus (“a physician, surgeon”), from medērī (“to heal”). Equivalent to medicate + -ion.

parole.significato: A substance which specifically promotes healing when ingested or consumed in some way; a pharmaceutical drug.
parole.testo: From Middle English medicin, from Middle French medicine, from Old French medecine, from Latin medicīna (“the healing art, medicine, a physician's shop, a remedy, medicine”), feminine of medicīnus (“of or belonging to physic or surgery, or to a physician or surgeon”), from medicus (“a physician, sur

parole.significato: The condition of being mediocre; having only an average degree of quality, skills etc.; no better than standard.
parole.testo: From Middle French médiocrité, from Latin mediocritās, from mediocris; by surface analysis, mediocre + -ity.

parole.significato: Lying, untruthful or dishonest.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French mendacieux, from Latin mendācium (“lie, untruth”), from mendāx (“lying”), + -ious.

parole.significato: located in the south, southern; later especially, often pertaining to the southern parts of Europe.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French meridional, from Latin merīdiōnālis, from merīdiēs (“noon; south”).

parole.significato: A mixed race person, especially if mostly white in ancestry, appearance and culture.

parole.testo: From Middle English metallyne, from Middle French metalin and Latin metallinus. By surface analysis, metal + -ine.

parole.testo: From Middle French métaphore, from Latin metaphora, from Ancient Greek μεταφορά (metaphorá), from μεταφέρω (metaphérō, “to transfer, apply”), from μετά (metá, “with, across, after”) + φέρω (phérō, “to bear, carry”).

parole.significato: A process by which a task is completed; a way of doing something (followed by the adposition of, to or for before the p…
parole.testo: From Middle French methode, from Latin methodus, from Ancient Greek μέθοδος (méthodos). By surface analysis, met- + -hod. See also -ode and hodo-.

parole.significato: A metropolis; the main city of a country or area.
parole.testo: From Middle English metropol, from Middle French metropole (“town with bishop's seat”), from Latin mētropolis. Doublet of metropolis.

parole.significato: An instance of moving to live in another place for a while.
parole.testo: From Middle French migration and its source, Latin migrātiō, from the participle stem of migrō (“to migrate”). Morphologically migrate + -ion.

parole.significato: a native or inhabitant of the ancient city of Miletus in Asia Minor.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French Milesien, and its source Latin Mīlēsius, from Ancient Greek Μιλήσιος (Milḗsios).

parole.significato: Fighting or disposed to fight; belligerent, warlike.
parole.testo: From Middle French militant, from Latin mīlitāns, present participle of mīlitāre (“to serve as a soldier”).

parole.significato: Any of a group of various types of grass or its grains used as food, widely cultivated in the developing world.
parole.testo: From late Middle English, borrowed from Middle French millet; from Latin milium, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *melh₂- (“to grind, crush”), see also Ancient Greek μελίνη (melínē, “millet”) and Lithuanian málnos (“millet”). Not related to مِلَّة (milla).

parole.significato: To attend to (the needs of); to tend; to take care (of); to give aid; to give service.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English mynystren, from Middle French ministrer, from Old French menistrer, ministrer and Latin ministrō, from minister.

parole.significato: In a state of misery: very sad, ill, or poor.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French miserable, from Old French, from Latin miserabilis, equivalent to miser + -able.

parole.significato: A reduction or decrease of something harmful or unpleasant.
parole.testo: From Middle French mitigation, from Latin mītigātiō.

parole.significato: The act or process of mixing; the state of being mixed or becoming mixed; a mixture.
parole.testo: From Middle French mixtion, mixion, and its source, Latin mixtiō, from mixtus (“mixed”).

parole.significato: The ability to move; capacity for movement.
parole.testo: From Middle French mobilité, and its source, Latin mōbilitās (“mobility”).

parole.significato: The state or quality of being moderate; avoidance of extremes.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French [Term?], from Old French moderacion, from Latin moderātiō. By surface analysis, moderate + ion.

parole.significato: Not bragging or boasting about oneself or one's achievements; unpretentious, humble.
parole.testo: From Middle French modeste, from Latin modestus.

parole.significato: The quality of being modest; having a limited and not overly high opinion of oneself and one's abilities.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French modestie, from Latin modestia; equivalent to modest + -y.

parole.significato: The act of assessing and prescribing a payment, penalty, price, valuation, etc.
parole.testo: From Middle English modificatioune, from Middle French modification and its etymon Latin modificātiō (“a measuring”), from modificāre (“to limit, control, modify”); see modify. By surface analysis, modify + -ication.

parole.significato: To change part of.
parole.testo: From Middle English modifien, from Middle French modifier, from Latin modificare (“to limit, control, regulate, deponent”), from modificari (“to measure off, set bound to, moderate”), from modus (“measure”) + facere (“to make”); see mode.

parole.significato: A fight or other contest between two people or forces; a duel; single combat.
parole.testo: From Middle French monomachie, or its source, Latin monomachia. Also mono- + -machy.

parole.significato: That causes disease; sickening, pathogenic.
parole.testo: From Middle French morbifique, or its source, post-classical morbificus, from Latin morbus (“sickness”).

parole.significato: The quality of being mordacious; biting severity, or sarcastic quality.
parole.testo: From Middle French mordacité (whence -acity), from Latin mordācitās (“quality of biting”), from mordāx (“biting, snappish, tart”), from mordeō (“bite, nibble”). Compare French mordacité. See mordacious.

parole.significato: A clasp or fastening used to fasten a cope in the front, usually decorative.
parole.testo: From Middle French mors, from Latin morsus (“bite; clasp”), from mordere (“to bite”).

parole.significato: The act of mortifying.
parole.testo: From Middle English mortificacioun, mortification, from Middle French mortification and its etymon Latin mortificātiō. By surface analysis, mortify + -ication.

parole.significato: Pertaining to Moses, or the writings and traditions attributed to him.
parole.testo: From Middle French mosaïque, moysaique, and its source, post-classical Latin Mosaicus (5th century), from Latin Moses, ultimately from Biblical Hebrew מֹשֶׁה (mōšê).

parole.significato: A fine or penalty, especially a pecuniary one.
parole.testo: From Middle French mulcter (“to fine, punish”), from Latin mulcta (“penalty, fine”). Possibly a doublet of milk.

parole.significato: The process of computing the sum of an addition with one and the same number a specified number of times (i.e. 4 times…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French, from Old French multiplicacion, from Latin multiplicatio, multiplicationem; ~equivalent to multiplicate + -ion.

parole.significato: The quality of being munificent; generosity.
parole.testo: From Middle French munificence, from Latin munificentia, from munus (“gift”) + facio (“to make”).

parole.significato: The mulberry fruit.
parole.testo: From Middle English murrey, murreye, from Middle French moré, morée, from Latin moratum, morata, from neuter and feminine respectively of moratus (“mulberry-colored”), from morum (“mulberry”) + -atus (“-ate”).

parole.significato: A black spot like an ermine spot, but without its three specks.
parole.testo: From Middle French mouscheture, from Latin musca (“a fly”).

parole.significato: A contractile form of tissue which animals use to effect movement.
parole.testo: From Middle English muscle, muscule, muskylle, and in part from Middle French muscle, from Latin mūsculus (“a muscle”, literally “little mouse”) because of the mouselike appearance of some muscles, from mūs (“mouse”). Doublet of mussel. More at mouse.

parole.significato: Made up of muscle or muscle tissue; muscular.
parole.testo: From late Middle English, from Middle French musculeux (“composed of muscle”), from Latin mūsculōsus (“muscular, fleshy”), from mūsculus (“a little mouse; a muscle”) + -ōsus (“-ous, -ose”, adjectival suffix).

parole.significato: Of a person: a source of inspiration.
parole.testo: From Middle French muse, from Latin Mūsa, from Ancient Greek Μοῦσα (Moûsa).

parole.significato: Having the same relationship, each to each other.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French mutuel, from Latin mūtuus. Displaced native Old English ġemǣne.

parole.significato: The collection of myths of a people, concerning the origin of the people, history, deities, ancestors and heroes.

parole.significato: Depicted swimming horizontally.
parole.testo: From Middle French noiant, present participle of noier (“to swim”), from Latin natare. Doublet of natant.

parole.significato: Narcissus.
parole.testo: From Middle French narcisse and its etymon Latin narcissus.

parole.significato: The act of recounting or relating in order the particulars of some action, occurrence, or affair; a narrating.
parole.testo: From Middle French narration, from Old French narracion, from Latin narrātiō. By surface analysis, Latin narr- + -ate + -ion.

parole.significato: A place built to stage a mock sea-battle, or the show performed therein.
parole.testo: From Middle French naumachie and its source, Latin naumachia.

parole.significato: Of or relating to a navy.
parole.testo: From Middle English naval, from Middle French naval, from Latin nāvālis; equivalent to navy + -al.

parole.significato: Capable of being navigated; deep enough and wide enough to afford passage to vessels.
parole.testo: From Middle French navigable, from Latin navigabilis.

parole.significato: The theory, practice and technology of charting a course for a road vehicle, ship, aircraft, or spaceship.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French navigation, from Latin nāvigātiōnem, accusative singular of nāvigātiō (“sailing, navigation”), from nāvigō (“sail”). Morphologically navigate + -ion.

parole.significato: In the form of a cloud or haze; hazy.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English nebulous, from Middle French nebuleus, from Latin nebulōsus (“full of mist, foggy, cloudy”), from nebula (“mist, vapour, cloud”), from Proto-Indo-European *nébʰos (“cloud, vapor, fog, moist, sky”). parole.significato: Synonym of negro or nigger.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French nègre, from Spanish and Portuguese negro, ultimately from Latin niger. Doublet of negro and noir.

parole.significato: Not taking sides in a conflict such as war; nonaligned.
parole.testo: From Middle French neutral (compare modern French neutre), from Latin neutrālis. By surface analysis, neuter + -al.

parole.significato: A nest of pheasants.
parole.testo: Uncertain; possibly from Middle French nid (modern French nid (“nest”)), or its etymon Latin nīdus (“nest”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *nisdós (“nest”)). Doublet of nest.

parole.significato: Pertaining to or composed of nitre; having the properties of nitre, bitter.
parole.testo: From Middle French nitreux, and its source, Latin nitrōsus (“nitrose”). Doublet of nitroso. By surface analysis, nitro- + -ous.

parole.significato: Of a person, creature, group, or species, primarily active during the night.
parole.testo: From Middle French nocturnal, from Latin nocturnālis (“nocturnal”), from Latin nocturnus (“nocturnal”), from Latin nox (“night”), from Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts (“night”). Cognates include Ancient Greek νύξ (núx), Sanskrit नक्ति (nákti), Old English niht (English night) and Proto-Slavic *noťь.

parole.significato: A member of a society or class who herd animals from pasture to pasture with no fixed home.
parole.testo: From Middle French nomade, from Latin Nomas (“wandering shepherd”), from Ancient Greek νομάς (nomás, “roaming, wandering, esp. to find pasture”), from Ancient Greek νομός (nomós, “pasture”). Compare Numidia.

parole.significato: An act or instance of nominating.
parole.testo: From Middle English nominacion, nomination, from Middle French nominacion and its etymon Latin nōminātiō, from the verb nōminō (“to name; to nominate”). By surface analysis, nominate + -ion.

parole.significato: The act of observing; perception.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French notice, from the Latin nōtitia. Doublet of notitia.

parole.significato: The act of notifying.
parole.testo: From Middle French notification, from Old French notificacion, from Latin nōtificātiō.

parole.significato: An infamous or notorious condition or reputation.
parole.testo: Derived from Middle French notoriété, from Medieval Latin nōtōrietās, from nōtōrius, from nōtus (“known”), perfect passive participle of nōscō (“get to know”). By surface analysis, notorious + -ety.

parole.significato: An innovation; a novelty.
