parole.significato: A non-existent or empty value or set of values.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French nul, from Latin nūllus.

parole.significato: Oral; not written.
parole.testo: From Middle English nuncupatif, nuncupatife, from Middle French nuncupatif and its etymon Latin nuncupātīvus (“nominal”).

parole.significato: The organic process by which an organism assimilates food and uses it for growth and maintenance.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French nutrition, from Old French nutricion, from Latin nutritio.

parole.significato: A tall, square, tapered, stone monolith topped with a pyramidal point, frequently used as a monument.
parole.testo: From Middle French obelisque, from Latin obeliscus (“obelisk”), from Ancient Greek ὀβελίσκος (obelískos), diminutive of ὀβελός (obelós, “needle”). Compare obelus.

parole.significato: The act of objecting.
parole.testo: From Middle French objection, from Old French objeccion, from Latin obiectio. Equivalent to object + -ion.

parole.significato: Not erect or perpendicular; not parallel to, or at right angles from, the base.
parole.testo: From Middle French oblique, from Latin oblīquus (also spelled oblīcus) (“slanting, sideways, indirect, envious”).

parole.testo: From Middle French obliquité, from Latin oblīquitās, from oblīquus (“oblique”). Corresponding to oblique + -ity.

parole.significato: Offensive to standards of decency or morality.
parole.testo: From Middle French obscene (modern French obscène (“indecent, obscene”)), and from its etymon Latin obscēnus, obscaenus (“inauspicious; ominous; disgusting, filthy; offensive, repulsive; indecent, lewd, obscene”). parole.significato: Darkness; the absence of light.
parole.testo: From Middle English obscurite, obscuryte, from Middle French obscurité and its etymon Latin obscūritās. By surface analysis, obscure + -ity.

parole.significato: The act of observing, and the fact of being observed (see observance)
parole.testo: From Middle English observacion, borrowed from Middle French observacion. Also a borrowing from French observation and a learned borrowing from Latin observātiō(n-). Morphologically observe + -ation.

parole.significato: An observer.
parole.testo: From Middle French observateur, from Latin observator, from the participle stem of observare.

parole.significato: To notice or view, especially carefully or with attention to detail.
parole.testo: From Middle French observer, from Old French observer, from Latin observō (“to watch”), from ob- (“before”) + servō (“to keep”), from Proto-Indo-European *ser- (“to guard”). Cognate with Gothic 𐍃𐌰𐍂𐍅𐌰 (sarwa, “weapons, armour”), Old English searu (“device”).

parole.significato: Disparagement, the belittling of someone or something; slander.
parole.testo: From Middle French obtrectacion and its source, Latin obtrectātiō (“disparagement”), from the participle stem of obtrectāre.

parole.significato: A favorable opportunity; a convenient or timely chance.
parole.testo: From Middle English occasioun, from Middle French occasion, from Old French occasiun, from Latin occāsiōnem, noun of action from perfect passive participle occāsus, from verb occidō, from prefix ob- (“down", "away”) + verb cadō (“fall”).

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or situated in, the occident, or west; western.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French occidental, from Latin occidentalis, equivalent to occident + -al.

parole.significato: A person who occupies an office or a position.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French occupant (present participle of occuper) or Latin occupāns, occupantis (present participle of occupō). By surface analysis, occupy + -ant.

parole.significato: An activity or task with which one occupies oneself; usually specifically the productive activity, service, trade, or c…
parole.testo: From Middle English occupacioun, borrowed from Middle French occupacion, occupation, from Latin occupātiō, occupātiōnis, from occupō (“occupy, seize”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kap- (“to seize, grab”). By surface analysis, occupy + -ation.

parole.significato: To happen or take place.
parole.testo: Originally "meet (in argument)", borrowed from Middle French occurrer, from Latin occurrō (“run to meet, run against, befall, present itself”) from prefix ob- (“against”) + verb currō (“run, hurry, move”).

parole.significato: Current, actual, occurring.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French occurrent and its source, Latin occurrēns.

parole.significato: To grant (a privilege etc, by a government etc).
parole.testo: From Middle English octroy, from Middle French octroyer, from Old French otroiier, from Latin auctōrizō. Doublet of authorize.

parole.significato: To hurt the feelings of; to displease; to make angry; to insult.
parole.testo: From Middle French offendre, from Latin offendō (“strike, blunder, commit an offense”), from ob- (“against”) + *fendō (“strike”).

parole.significato: Causing offense; arousing a visceral reaction of disgust, anger, hatred, sadness, or indignation.
parole.testo: From Middle French offensif, from offendre + -if by analogy with défensif. Offendre is from Latin offendere (“to offend”); see offend.

parole.significato: The sense of smell; the detection of airborne molecules.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French olfaction /olefaction, from Latin olfactus, perfect passive participle of olfaciō (“to smell (transitive)”) + -tion.

parole.significato: Imposing or constituting a physical, mental, or figurative load which can be borne only with effort; burdensome.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English onerous, borrowed from Middle French onereux, from Old French onereus, a learned borrowing from Latin onerosus, from onus (“burden”) + -ōsus. Compare exonerate.

parole.significato: Effectual or important.
parole.testo: From Middle English operative, operatyfe, from Middle French operatif (modern French opératif) or its etymon Latin operātīvus. By surface analysis, operate + -ive.

parole.significato: To express an opinion; to state as an opinion; to suppose, consider (that).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French opiner, from Latin opīnor (“to hold as an opinion”), from *opīnus (“thinking, expecting”), only in negative nec-opīnus (“not expecting”) and in-opīnus (“not expected”); akin to optō (“to choose, desire”), and to apīscor (“to obtain”); see optate and opt.

parole.significato: A chance for advancement, progress or profit.
parole.testo: From opportune + -ity, from Middle French opportunité, from Latin opportūnitās.

parole.significato: To contradict or controvert; to oppose; to challenge or question the truth or validity of a given statement.
parole.testo: From Middle French oppugner Latin oppugno (“fight against, to attack, assail, assault, storm, besiege, war with”).

parole.significato: A small or petty work.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French opuscule, from Latin opusculum, diminutive of opus. Compare opuscle, opusculum. Equivalent to opus + -cule.

parole.significato: The gold or yellow tincture on a coat of arms.
parole.testo: From late Middle English or (“gold”), borrowed from Middle French or (“yellow”), from Old French or, from Latin aurum (“gold”). Doublet of aurum.

parole.significato: The act of ordaining or the state of being ordained.
parole.testo: From Middle French ordination, from Old French ordinacion, from Latin ordinatio.

parole.significato: Any of various colourful passerine birds, New World orioles of the genus Icterus (family Icteridae) and Old World oriol…
parole.testo: A borrowing from Middle French oriol, from Old French oriol, from Latin aureolus, diminutive of aureus (“golden”). Doublet of aureole. First use appears c. 1776 in the writings of Thomas Pennant.

parole.significato: A small European migratory bunting (Emberiza hortulana), once eaten whole as a delicacy.
parole.testo: From Middle French hortolan (“gardener”), from Latin hortulānus (“gardener”). Doublet of hortulan.

parole.significato: Either of the horn-like protuberances on the heads of giraffes and male okapi. Some extinct species in the family bore…
parole.testo: From Latin os (“bone”) and Middle French cone, from Latin cōnus (“cone, wedge, peak”), from Ancient Greek κῶνος (kônos, “cone, spinning top, pine cone”).

parole.significato: Gypaetus barbatus, the bearded vulture, the diet of which is almost exclusively bone marrow.
parole.testo: From Middle French ossifrage, from Latin ossifraga (“osprey”), ossifragus (“osprey”), from ossifragus (“bone breaking”).

parole.significato: The act of presenting an ostensive definition.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French ostension, in turn from Latin ostensiō, ostensiōnem.

parole.significato: To make an ambitious display of; to exhibit or show boastingly; to ostentate.

parole.significato: A portent, a token.
parole.testo: From Middle French ostente (“amazing or marvellous thing; prodigy, wonder”) or directly from its etymon Latin ostentum (“portent”), from ostendere (“to exhibit, show”); see further at etymology 1. The plural form ostenta is from Latin ostenta.

parole.significato: Ambitious display; vain show; display intended to excite admiration or applause.
parole.testo: Originated 1425–75 from late Middle English ostentacioun, borrowed from Middle French ostentation and its etymon Latin ostentātiō, ostentātiōnem, equivalent to ostentātus (past participle of ostentāre, to display or exhibit), frequentative of ostendere (“to present, display”) + -iōn. By surface anal

parole.significato: The state or quality of being otiose.
parole.testo: From otiose + -ity, from Middle French ociosité, from Latin otiositas, from Latin otiosus + -itas (“-ity”).

parole.significato: An avoirdupois ounce, weighing ¹⁄₁₆ of an avoirdupois pound, or 28.349523125 grams.
parole.testo: From Middle English ounce, unce, from Middle French once, from Latin ū̆ncia (“Roman ounce, various similar units”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *óynos (“one”). Doublet of a, one, inch, uncia, onça, onza, oka, ouguiya, and awqiyyah.

parole.significato: To bring peace to (a place or situation), by ending (or suppressing) war, fighting, violence, anger or agitation.
parole.testo: From Middle French pacifier, from Latin pāx (“peace”) + faciō (“to do, make”). Cognate with pay and peacify.

parole.significato: An agreement; a compact; a covenant.
parole.testo: From Middle English pact, from Middle French pacte, from Old French, and its etymon Latin pactum (“something agreed upon”), from pacīscī (“to agree”).

parole.significato: To mark or number the pages of, as a book or manuscript.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French page, from Latin pāgina, from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂ǵ-. Doublet of pagina.

parole.significato: An ode or other poem in which the author retracts something said in an earlier poem; (loosely) a recantation.
parole.testo: From Middle French palinod, from Latin palinōdia (“palinode, recantation”), from Ancient Greek παλινῳδία (palinōidía, “palinode”), from πάλιν (pálin, “again”) + ᾠδή (ōidḗ, “song”).

parole.significato: A narrow vertical stripe, narrower than a pale. Diminutive of pale.
parole.testo: Said to be from Middle English *palet, from Middle French *palet, from Middle French pal (“pale”), ultimately from Latin palla (“a strip of cloth”).

parole.significato: The alleviation of a disease's symptoms without a cure; temporary relief.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French palliation, from Latin palliare (“to cloak; to conceal”), from Latin pallium (“cloak”). By surface analysis, palliate + -ion.

parole.significato: Capable of being touched, felt or handled; touchable, tangible.
parole.testo: From Middle French palpable and its source, Latin palpābilis, which is from palpō (“to touch softly”) + -bilis.

parole.significato: An abnormal beating of the heart that may be perceived by the patient, a result of excitement, exertion, or illness.
parole.testo: From Middle French palpitation, from Latin palpitatio.

parole.significato: A small, brief printed work, consisting either of a folded sheet of paper, or several sheets bound together into a book…
parole.testo: The noun is derived from Late Middle English pamflet, pamphilet (“short written text; small book; tract”) [and other forms], from Middle French Pamphilet (compare Late Latin (Anglo-Latin) pamfletus, panfletus, paunflettus (“short written text”), Old French Panfilès), a popular shorthand for the 12th

parole.significato: A Roman Catholic, especially one whose loyalties are seen to be with the papacy in Rome.
parole.testo: From Middle French papiste, from Latin pāpa (“pope”).

parole.significato: An apparently self-contradictory statement, which can only be true if it is false, and vice versa.
parole.testo: From Middle French paradoxe, from Latin paradoxum, from Ancient Greek παράδοξος (parádoxos, “unexpected, strange”).

parole.significato: A passage in text that starts on a new line, the first line sometimes being indented, and usually marks a change of top…
parole.testo: From Middle English paragraf, from Middle French paragraphe from Latin paragraphus (“sign for start of a new section of discourse”), from Ancient Greek παράγραφος (parágraphos), from παρά (pará, “beside”) and γράφω (gráphō, “to write”). Doublet of paragraphos.

parole.significato: Equally distant from one another at all points.
parole.testo: From Middle French parallèle and its etymon Latin parallēlus, parallēlos. The verb is from the noun. See also para- and allo-.

parole.significato: A friend of the bridegroom; a best man; a bridesmaid.
parole.testo: From Middle French paranymphe, from Latin paranymphus, from Ancient Greek παράνυμφος (paránumphos, “friend of bridegroom”), from παρα- (para-, “para-”) + νύμφη (númphē, “bride”).

parole.significato: A restatement of a text in different words, often to clarify meaning or from memory rather than verbatim.
parole.testo: From Middle French paraphrase, from Latin paraphrasis, from Ancient Greek παράφρασις (paráphrasis), equivalent to para- + phrase. Doublet of paraphrasis.

parole.significato: An organism that lives on or in another organism of a different species, deriving benefit from living on or in that oth…
parole.testo: From Middle French parasite, from Latin parasitus, from Ancient Greek παράσιτος (parásitos, “person who eats at the table of another”), from noun use of adjective meaning "feeding beside", from παρά (pará, “beside”) + σῖτος (sîtos, “food”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to a parent.
parole.testo: From Middle French parental, from Latin parentālis, from parens (“parent”).

parole.significato: Word of mouth.
parole.testo: from Middle French parole, from Latin parabola, from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ). Doublet of parable.

parole.significato: Someone who kills a relative, especially a parent.
parole.testo: From Middle French parricide, from Latin parricīda, of uncertain origin, perhaps from pār (“equal”).

parole.significato: The killing of a relative, especially a parent.
parole.testo: From Middle French parricide, from Latin parricīdium, of uncertain origin, perhaps from pār (“equal”).

parole.significato: One who participates.
parole.testo: From stem of particip(ate) + -ant, borrowed from Middle French participant, from Latin participāns, present participle of participō; see participate. Displaced native Old English dǣlnimend (literally “part taker”).

parole.significato: A very small piece of matter, a fragment; especially, the smallest possible part of something.
parole.testo: From Middle French particule, and its source, Latin particula (“small part, particle”), diminutive of pars (“part, piece”). Semantically displaced native Old English grot whence modern English groat.

parole.significato: Being subjected to an action without producing a reaction.
parole.testo: From Middle English passyf, passyve, from Middle French, French passif, from Latin passivus (“serving to express the suffering of an action; in late Latin literally capable of suffering or feeling”), from passus, past participle of pati (“to suffer”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peh₁- (“to

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to shepherds or herders of other livestock.
parole.testo: From Middle French, Old French pastoral, from Latin pāstōrālis, from pāstor (“shepherd”), + adjective suffix -ālis.

parole.significato: Fatherhood, the state or quality of being a father.
parole.testo: From Middle French paternité, from Old French, from Latin paternitās (“paternity”), from paternus (“of or pertaining to a father, paternal”) + -itās, from pater (“father”).

parole.significato: Arousing pity, sympathy, or compassion; exciting pathos.
parole.testo: From Middle French pathétique, from Latin patheticus, from Ancient Greek παθητικός (pathētikós, “subject to feeling, capable of feeling, impassioned”), from παθητός (pathētós, “one who has suffered, subject to suffering”), from πάσχω (páskhō, “to suffer”). By surface analysis, path- + -etic.

parole.significato: Willing to wait if necessary; not losing one's temper while waiting.
parole.testo: From Middle English pacient, from Middle French patient, from Old French pacient, from Latin patiens, present participle of patior (“to suffer, endure”), from Proto-Indo-European *peh₁- (“to hate, hurt”).

parole.significato: A member of any of the families constituting the populus Romanus, or body of Roman citizens, before the development of…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French patricien, from Latin patricius, derived from patrēs cōnscrīptī (“Roman senators”). May also have been derived from Latin patricius + -ian

parole.significato: The murder of one's father.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French patricide or Latin patricīdium. Equivalent to patri- + -cide.

parole.significato: One who has murdered their father.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French patricide or Latin patricīda. Equivalent to patri- + -cide.

parole.significato: A right or estate inherited from one's father; or, in a larger sense, from any male ancestor.
parole.testo: From earlier patrimoyne, from patremoyne, from Middle French patrimoine/patremoine, semilearned borrowing from Latin patrimōnium, from pater (“father”) + -mōnium (“state, condition”). First attested in 1513. By surface analysis, patri- + -mony. Compare matrimony. Displaced native Old English fæderġe

parole.significato: Fewness in number; too few.
parole.testo: From Middle English paucete, paucite, paucyte, partly from Middle French paucité and partly from its etymon, Latin paucitās (“a small number, fewness, scarcity”), from paucus (“few, little”). Related to few.

parole.significato: To take a temporary rest, take a break for a short period after an effort.
parole.testo: From Middle French pause, from Latin pausa, from Ancient Greek παῦσις (paûsis), from Ancient Greek παύω (paúō, “stop”), of uncertain origin. Doublet of pausa.

parole.significato: A teacher or instructor of children; one whose occupation is to teach the young.
parole.testo: From Middle English pedagoge, from Middle French pedagogue, from Latin paedagōgus, from Ancient Greek παιδαγωγός (paidagōgós), from παῖς (paîs, “child”) + ἀγωγός (agōgós, “guide”) (from ἄγω (ágō, “lead”)). By surface analysis, ped- (“child”) + -agogue.

parole.significato: A legal sentence.
parole.testo: From Middle French pénalité, from pénal, from Latin poenālis, from poena, borrowing of Ancient Greek ποινή (poinḗ), from Proto-Hellenic *kʷoinā́, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷoynéh₂, comprising *kʷey- + *-néh₂.

parole.significato: The organisation, identification and interpretation of sensory information.
parole.testo: From Middle English percepcioun, from Middle French percepcion, from Latin perceptiō (“a receiving or collecting, perception, comprehension”), from perceptus (“perceived, observed”), perfect passive participle of percipiō (“to perceive, observe”); see perceive.

parole.significato: The collision of two bodies in order to produce a sound.
parole.testo: From Middle English percussioun, from Middle French, Old French percussion, from Latin percussiō (“striking”), from percutiō (“to strike”).

parole.significato: A state or act of violating faith or allegiance; violation of a promise or vow, or of trust.
parole.testo: From Middle French perfidie, from Latin perfidia from perfidus (“faithless, treacherous, false”), from fides (“faith”); related to, for example, English fidelity.

parole.significato: The act of perfusing, the passage of fluid through the circulatory system.
parole.testo: From Middle French perfusion, from Latin perfūsiō (“the act of pouring over”).

parole.significato: The outside boundary, parts or surface of something.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French peripherie. Compare Middle English periferie (“one of three layers of atmosphere (lower, middle, and upper) believed to surround the Earth”), from the same origin, although the Modern English term most likely does not descend from it.

parole.significato: Without end, eternal.
parole.testo: From Middle English permanent, permanente, from Middle French permanent, from Latin permanēns, from permaneō (“to stay through”). First attested in the 15th century.

parole.significato: authorisation; consent (especially formal consent from someone in authority)
parole.testo: From Middle English permision, permission, permissioun, permyssion, from Middle French permission, from Latin permissiō. Equivalent to permit + -ion. Mostly replaced native English leave, from Old English lēaf (“permission”).

parole.significato: To allow (something) to happen, to give permission for.
parole.testo: From Middle English permitten, borrowed from Middle French permettre, from Latin permittō (“give up, allow”), from per (“through”) + mittō (“send”).

parole.significato: At or forming a right angle (to something).
parole.testo: Derived from Middle French perpendiculaire, from Old French perpendiculer, from Latin perpendiculum (“plumb line”).

parole.significato: The state or quality of being perplexed.
parole.testo: From Middle English perplexite, borrowed from Middle French perplexité or post-classical Latin perplexitās, from perplexus (“entangled”). By surface analysis, perplex + -ity.

parole.significato: Enduring; persistent, resistant.
parole.testo: From Middle English perseveraunt, from Middle French perseverant, from Latin persevērāns, present participle of persevērō.

parole.significato: To go on stubbornly or resolutely.
parole.testo: From Middle French persister (Modern French persister), from Latin persistere, from per- + sistere (“to stand”).

parole.significato: The property of being persistent.
parole.testo: From Middle French persistance, from persistant, from Latin persistēns, from persistō. By surface analysis, persist + -ence.

parole.significato: Of people, a set of non-physical psychological and social qualities that make one person distinct from another.
parole.testo: From Middle English personalite, from Middle French [Term?], from Latin persōnālitās. First attested in the late 14th century. By surface analysis, personal + -ity.

parole.significato: Acute discernment or understanding; insight.
parole.testo: From Middle French perspicacité (whence -acity) or directly from Latin perspicācitās (“sharpsightedness, discrimination”), from perspicāx (“sharp-sighted”), from perspicio, from per- + specio, "see through (something)".

parole.significato: The action or process of perspiring.
parole.testo: Borrowed from late Middle French perspiration, from perspirer (“perspire”), from Latin perspirare (“to blow or breathe constantly”), from per (“through”) + spirare (“to breathe, blow”). Morphologically perspire + -ation.

parole.significato: To emit (sweat or perspiration) through the skin's pores.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French perspirer and its source Latin perspīrō (“to breathe everywhere, blow constantly”), from per (“through”) + spīrō (“to breathe”); see spirit.

parole.significato: Agitation; the state of being perturbed.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French perturbation, from Old French perturbacion, from Latin perturbatio.

parole.significato: The quality of being perverse.
parole.testo: From perverse + -ity, from Middle French perversité, from Latin perversitās.

parole.significato: A pestilence, i.e. a deadly epidemic, a deadly plague.
parole.testo: In the 16th century in the sense of "pestilence" and specifically bubonic plague from Middle French peste (“pestilence”) (whence French peste). The other meanings are recorded soon after. Ultimately from Latin pestis.

parole.significato: A short but large-caliber, heavy 16th- and 17th-century firearm that used a matchlock or wheellock mechanism, intermedi…
parole.testo: From Middle French petrinal, alteration of poitrinal, from poitrinal (“of the chest”) (the weapon is thought to have been braced against a chest-pad when firing), from poitrine (“chest, breast”), from Latin pectorina, feminine of pectorinus (“of the breast”) (from pectus (“chest”) + -inus (“-ine”)).

parole.significato: Resembling rock or stone in its hardness.
parole.testo: From Middle English, borrowed from Middle French petreux, from Latin petrōsus, from petra, from Ancient Greek πέτρα (pétra).

parole.significato: Rudeness, insolence.
parole.testo: From Middle French pétulance, and its source, Latin petulantia.

parole.significato: Childishly irritable.
parole.testo: From Middle French, from Latin petulāns, akin to petō (“to ask for”).

parole.significato: Synonym of phalanx (“group of soldiers, people etc.”).
parole.testo: From Middle English phalange, from Middle French phalange, from Old French phalange, from Latin phalanx (accusative phalangem), from Ancient Greek φάλαγξ (phálanx). Doublet of phalanx, planch, plancha, planche, and plank.

parole.significato: A philologist.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French philologue, from Latin philologus (“lover of learning”), from Ancient Greek φιλολόγος (philológos, “lover of words and learning”). Equivalent to philo- + -logue.

parole.significato: Reverence and devotion to God.
parole.testo: From Middle English piete, borrowed from Middle French pieté, from Latin pietās. See also the doublets pietà and pity. By surface analysis, pious + -ety.

parole.significato: A large farm; estate or area of land designated for agricultural growth. Often includes housing for the owner and worke…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French plantation, from Latin plantātiō (“planting, transplanting”), from plantātus (“planted”), the perfect passive participle of plantāre, + action noun suffix -tiō.

parole.significato: An act of folding.
parole.testo: From Middle French plicacion, and its source, Latin plicatio.

parole.significato: The feathers covering the body of a bird collectively.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English plumage, plummage (“bird’s feathers collectively, plumage; (falconry) feathers fed to a hawk to cause it to regurgitate, casting”), from Middle French plumage, plomage (“bird’s feathers collectively; person’s (showy) clothing”), from Old French plumage (“bird’s feathers coll

parole.significato: A literary piece written in verse.
parole.testo: From Middle French poème, from Latin poēma, from Ancient Greek ποίημα (poíēma), from ποιέω (poiéō, “to make”). Widely displaced English leed.

parole.significato: Relating to poetry.
parole.testo: From Middle French poetique, from Latin poeticus, from Ancient Greek ποιητικός (poiētikós) from ποιέω (poiéō, “make”). Displaced native Old English sċoplīċ and lēoþlīċ. Doublet of poietic.

parole.significato: Either of the two points on the earth's surface around which it rotates; also, similar points on any other rotating obj…
parole.testo: From Middle French pole, pôle, from Latin polus, from Ancient Greek πόλος (pólos, “axis of rotation”).

parole.significato: To enforce the law and keep order among (a group).
parole.testo: From Middle French police, from Latin polītīa (“state, government”), from Ancient Greek πολιτεία (politeía). Doublet of policy, polis (“police”), and polity.

parole.significato: Of or relating to polity, or civil government; political.
parole.testo: From Middle French politique, from Latin polīticus, from Ancient Greek πολιτικός (politikós), from πολίτης (polítēs, “citizen”). Cognate with German politisch (“political”). Doublet of politico.

parole.significato: Organizational structure and governance, especially of a state or a religion.
parole.testo: From Middle French politie, from Latin polītīa, from Ancient Greek πολιτεία (politeía, “polity, policy, the state”). Doublet of police, policy, and polis (“police”).

parole.significato: A dagger typically having a slender square or triangular blade.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French poignard (whence -ard), from poing (“fist”), from Old French poing, from Latin pugnus (“fist”).

parole.significato: A member of the most illustrious of the colleges of priests of the Roman religion, the College of Pontiffs; a pontifex.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French pontife m, from Latin pontifex m. Doublet of pontifex.

parole.significato: A flat-bottomed boat or other floating structure used as a buoyant support for a temporary bridge, dock or landing stag…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French ponton, from Old French ponton, from Latin pontō, pontōnem (“ferryboat”), from pōns (“bridge”).

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or being a pig.
parole.testo: From Middle English porcine, partly from Middle French porcin (from Old French [Term?]) and partly from its etymon, Latin porcīnus, from porcus (“pig”).

parole.significato: Able to be carried or easily moved.
parole.testo: From Middle English portable, from Middle French portable and Latin portābilis. By surface analysis, port (“to carry”) + -able.

parole.significato: The manner in which one carries oneself; behaviour.
parole.testo: From Middle French portance (“a carrying, support”), from porter (“to carry”), from Latin portare (“carry, bear, convey”).

parole.significato: A Portuguese person.
parole.testo: From Middle English Portyngale, from Middle French Portingal, which added an intrusive /n/ sound through the process of excrescence, from Latin Portucale.

parole.significato: A large travelling case usually made of leather, and opening into two equal sections.
parole.testo: From Middle French portemanteau (“coat stand”), from porte (“he carries”, third-person singular present indicative of porter (“to carry”)) + manteau (“coat”), literally “[that which] carries coat”. The lexical sense (sense 2) was first used figuratively by Lewis Carroll in Through the Looking-Glass

parole.significato: A painting or other picture of a person, especially the head and shoulders.
parole.testo: From Middle French portraict, pourtraict, nominal use of the past participle of portraire (“portray”), from Latin prōtrahō (< prō- + trahō). Compare typologically English drawing.

parole.significato: To have (something) as, or as if as, an owner; to have, to own.
parole.testo: PIE word  *pótis From Middle English possessen (“to have, own; to obtain possession of; to inhabit, occupy”) [and other forms], from Middle French possesser, possessier, Old French possesser, possessier (“to have, own, possess; to dominate”), from Latin possessus (“possessed; seized”), the perfect p

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to ownership or possession.
parole.testo: From Middle French possessif, from Latin possessivus (“of or pertaining to possession”), from possessiō (“possessing”), from possidēre (“to possess”). By surface analysis, possess + -ive.

parole.significato: All the future generations, especially the descendants of a specific person.
parole.testo: Late 14th century, from Middle French posterité, from Latin posteritas, from posterus (“following, coming after”), from post (“after”) (English post-).

parole.significato: Perversion, depravity; wickedness.
parole.testo: From Middle French pravité, and its source, Latin prāvitās (“crookedness; depravity”), from prāvus (“prave”).

parole.significato: To go before, go in front of.
parole.testo: From Middle French précéder, from Latin praecēdō, from prae- + cēdō.

parole.significato: An act in the past which may be used as an example to help decide the outcome of similar instances in the future.
parole.testo: From Middle French, from Old French, from Latin praecēdēns, present participle of praecēdere (“to precede”); See precede.

parole.significato: The quality of being overly refined in an affected way (often used to describe speech or writing, but also visual art a…
parole.testo: From Middle English preciosite, from Middle French preciosité, from Latin pretiōsitās (“great value; high price”).

parole.significato: A very steep cliff.
parole.testo: First attested in 1598, from Middle French precipice, from Latin praecipitium (“a steep place”), from praeceps (“steep”), from prae + caput (“head”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kap- (“head”). Distantly related to precept through Latin praecipiō (“to teach”), from prae + capiō (“take”), ult

parole.significato: Any or all of the forms of water particles, whether liquid or solid, that fall from the upper atmosphere (e.g., rain, h…
parole.testo: From Middle French précipitation, from Latin praecipitātiō, praecipitātiōnem. By surface analysis, precipitate + -ion.

parole.significato: Both exact and accurate.
parole.testo: From Middle French précis, from Latin praecīsus, perfect passive participle of praecīdere, from prae- (“before, in front”) + caedere (“cut; strike”), cognate with hit. Related to incise. Doublet of précis.

parole.significato: Knowledge of the future; understanding of something in advance, especially as a form of supernatural or extrasensory pe…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French precognition or its source, Latin praecognitio, from praecognōscō (“to know beforehand”). Doublet of Germanic-based foreknowledge and Greek-based prognosis. Equivalent to pre- + cognition.

parole.significato: That which precurses: a forerunner, predecessor, or indicator of approaching events.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English precursour, from Middle French precurseur or its etymon Latin praecursor (“forerunner”). By surface analysis, precurse + -or.

parole.significato: Exceeding others in quality or rank; of outstanding excellence, extremely notable or important.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French preeminent and its source, Latin praeēminēns, present participle of praeēmineō (“to stand out, excel”), from prae- (“pre-”) + ēmineō.

parole.significato: The office or position of a prefect.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French préfecture, from Latin praefectūra. Equivalent to prefect + -ure. As an East Asian administrative division, a calque of Chinese 府 (fǔ) and 郡 (jùn), also used to describe 縣 /县 (xian, “county”) and 州 (zhou, “province”) in some eras.

parole.significato: To determine beforehand; to set in advance.
parole.testo: From Middle English prefixen, from Middle French prefixer, from Latin praefīxus, past participle of praefīgō (“to (fix, fasten, set up) in front”, “to fix on the (end, extremity)”) (from prae- (“before”) + fīgō (“to fix”, “to fasten”, “to affix”)), equivalent to pre- + -fix.

parole.significato: Compelling; clear, evident.
parole.testo: Apparently from Middle French pregnant, preignant (“pressing, compelling”), present participle of prembre (“to press”), from Latin premere (“to press”).

parole.significato: Existing previously, preexistent.
parole.testo: Multiple origins. Borrowed from Middle French prejacent (“previously existing”) during the sixteenth century. Also attested in twelfth century British sources, from post-classical Latin praeiacens (“situated before”).

parole.significato: To form a judgment of (something) in advance.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French préjuger, itself an adaptation of Latin praeudico, praeiudicare. Doublet of prejudicate.

parole.significato: Foremost; first or highest in quality or degree.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French premier (adjective), from Latin prīmārius. Doublet of primary.

parole.significato: The state of being preoccupied or an idea that preoccupies the mind; enthrallment.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French préoccupation, from Latin praeoccupātiō. By surface analysis, pre- + occupation or preoccupy + -ation.

parole.significato: To distract; to draw attention elsewhere.
parole.testo: From pre- + occupy, after Middle French preoccuper, and its source, Latin praeoccupo, praeoccupare. Doublet of preoccupate, now obsolete.

parole.significato: The act of preparing or getting ready.
parole.testo: From Middle English preparacion, from Middle French preparacion, from Latin praeparatio, praeparationem. Morphologically prepare + -ation.

parole.significato: To make ready for a specific future purpose; to set up; to assemble or equip; to forearm.

parole.significato: A moon or other smaller body orbiting a larger one.

parole.significato: The state of being satiated.

parole.significato: A type of fine cloth similar to serge.

parole.significato: A beetle of the species Scarabaeus sacer, sacred to the ancient Egyptians.

parole.significato: The location of an event that attracts attention.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a schism.

parole.significato: A member of the medieval philosophical school of scholasticism; a medieval Christian Aristotelian.

parole.significato: Exactly and carefully conducted.

parole.significato: In a careful manner, with scruple; done with careful attention to detail.

parole.significato: To transfer temporarily to alternative employment.

parole.significato: The condition of not being threatened, especially physically, psychologically, emotionally, or financially.

parole.significato: Not moving; relatively still; staying in the vicinity.

parole.significato: A collection of small particles, particularly dirt, that precipitates from a river or other body of water.
parole.testo: From Middle French sédiment, from Latin sedimentum < sedeō.

parole.significato: Of, related to, or being involved in sedition.

parole.significato: The act of seducing.

parole.significato: One who seduces.

parole.significato: The decision or judgement of a jury or court; a verdict.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French sentence, from Latin sententia (“way of thinking, opinion, sentiment”), from sentiēns, present participle of sentiō (“to feel, think”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sent- (“to feel”).

parole.significato: Able to be separated.
parole.testo: From Middle English separable, from Middle French separable and its etymon Latin sēparābilis.

parole.significato: The events, collectively, which follow a previously mentioned event; the aftermath.
parole.testo: From Middle English sequele, sequelle, sequile, from Middle French sequele, sequelle and its etymon, Latin sequēla, from sequī (“to follow”). Doublet of sequela.

parole.significato: That comes after in time or order; subsequent.
parole.testo: 1550s; borrowed from Middle French sequent, from Old French sequent, itself borrowed from Latin sequentem, present participle of sequī (“to follow”).

parole.significato: The state of being a slave; slavery; being forced to work for others or do their bidding without one's consent or again…
parole.testo: From Middle French servitude, from Latin servitūdō, from Latin servus (“slave”). Equivalent to serve + -itude.

parole.significato: Synonym of sestertius.

parole.significato: Very bad or intense.

parole.significato: The state of being severe.

parole.significato: The extent to which something matters; importance
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English significaunce, from Middle French significance, from Old French significance, from Latin significantia. Doublet of signifiance.

parole.significato: Something that simulates a system or environment in order to predict actual behaviour.

parole.significato: Genuine, honest, and free from pretense or deceit; heartfelt.

parole.significato: Tending to socialize or be social.

parole.significato: the action or instance of soliciting; petition; proposal
parole.testo: From Middle French sollicitation, from Latin sollicitātiō.

parole.significato: The state or quality of being solid.

parole.significato: To sprinkle or spray.

parole.significato: A ghostly apparition, a phantom.

parole.significato: A pin or peg used to stop the vent in a cask.

parole.significato: A small copse or wood, especially one planted as a shelter for game birds.

parole.significato: Unable to reproduce (or procreate).

parole.significato: Having or revealing little emotion or sensibility.

parole.significato: To suppress (in various senses).
parole.testo: From Middle English supprymen, from Middle French supprimer and its etymon Latin supprimere, supprimō (“to press down, suppress”), from sub- (“under, down”) + premō (“to press”).

parole.significato: Tangible; perceptible to the sense of touch.

parole.significato: Retaliation; retribution.

parole.significato: A person's usual manner of thinking, behaving or reacting.

parole.significato: The quality or state of being tenacious, or persistence of purpose; tenaciousness.
parole.testo: From Middle French ténacité, from Latin tenācitās (whence -acity).

parole.significato: To make a tender of; to offer or tender.

parole.significato: A thin, spirally coiling stem that attaches a plant to its support.
parole.testo: From Middle French tendrillon (“bud, shoot, cartilage”), perhaps a diminutive of tendron (“cartilage”), from Old French tendre (“soft”) (see tender (adjective)), or else from Latin tendere (“to stretch, extend”) (see tender (verb)).

parole.significato: The condition of being held in a state between two or more forces, which are acting in opposition to each other.

parole.significato: To settle, determine.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French terminer, from Latin termināre. Doublet of terminate.

parole.significato: To frighten greatly; to fill with terror.
parole.testo: From Middle French terrifier, from Latin terrificare.

parole.significato: Intense dread, fright, or fear.
parole.testo: From late Middle English terrour, from Old French terreur f (“terror, fear, dread”), from Latin terror (“fright, fear, terror”), from terrēre (“to frighten, terrify”), from Old Latin tr̥reō, from Proto-Italic *trozeō, from Proto-Indo-European *tre- (“to shake”), *tres- (“to tremble”).

parole.significato: The feel or shape of a surface or substance; the smoothness, roughness, softness, etc. of something.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French texture, borrowed from Latin textūra (“a weaving, web, texture, structure”), from textus, past participle of texere (“to weave”). See text. Doublet of tessitura.

parole.significato: The study of God, a god, or gods; and of the truthfulness of religion in general.
parole.testo: From Middle English theologie, from Middle French theologie, from Old French theologie, from Latin theologia, from Koine Greek θεολογία (theología), from θεολόγος (theológos, adjective), from θεός (theós) + λόγος (lógos). By surface analysis, theo- + -logy.

parole.significato: A type of inflorescence; a compact panicle having an obscured main axis and cymose subaxes.
parole.testo: From Middle French thyrse, from Latin thyrsus, from Ancient Greek θύρσος (thúrsos). Doublet of thyrsus, torse, and torso.

parole.significato: Lacking in courage or confidence.
parole.testo: From Middle French timide, from Latin timidus (“full of fear, fearful, timid”), from timeō (“to fear”).

parole.significato: The state of being timid; shyness.
parole.testo: From timid + -ity, from Middle French timidité, from Latin timiditātem.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, being, derived from, or having a title.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French titulaire, from Latin titulāris, from titulus (“title”).

parole.significato: A toga.
parole.testo: From Middle English toge, from Middle French toge and Latin toga. Doublet of toga and tog.

parole.significato: Capable of being borne, tolerated or endured; bearable or endurable.

parole.significato: Endurance of evil, suffering etc.

parole.significato: One in a series of volumes.
parole.testo: From Middle French tome, from Latin tomus (“section of larger work”), from Ancient Greek τόμος (tómos, “section, roll of papyrus, volume”), from τέμνω (témnō, “to cut, separate”).

parole.significato: A twist of cloth or wreath, typically placed underneath and forming part of a crest (as an orle or wreath) and customar…
parole.testo: From Middle French torse (“wreath”), from Latin torqueō (“to twist”). Doublet of trousse and truss.

parole.significato: An identifying characteristic, habit or trend.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French trait (“line, feature”), from Latin tractus (“drawing, pulling”), from Latin trahō. Doublet of tract.

parole.significato: Free from emotional or mental disturbance.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French tranquille, from Latin tranquillus, from trāns- + the root of quiēs (“rest, quiet, peace”), ultimately from *kʷyeh₁- (“to rest”).

parole.significato: The act or process of transcribing, or converting spoken (or sometimes signed) language to the written form.
parole.testo: From Middle French transcription, or directly from Latin transcriptiōnem, from trānscrībō (“transcribe”).

parole.significato: To render motionless, by arousing terror, amazement or awe.
parole.testo: From Middle French transfixer, from Old French transfixer, from Latin transfigō (“to pierce through”), from trans- (“through”) + figō (“to pierce”).

parole.significato: To change greatly the appearance or form of.
parole.testo: From Middle English transformen, from Old French transformer, from Latin transformo, transformare, from trans (“across”, preposition) + forma (“form”).

parole.significato: The process of change from one form, state, style or place to another.
parole.testo: From Middle French transition, from Latin transitio. By surface analysis, transit + -ion.

parole.significato: Lasting only a short time; temporary.
parole.testo: From Middle French transitoire, from Old French, from Latin trānsitōrius.

parole.significato: To transmute, change.
parole.testo: From Middle French transmuer, from Latin transmūtāre.

parole.significato: A crossbeam.

parole.significato: A grandfather's grandfather; a great-great-grandfather.

parole.testo: From Middle English trine, from Middle French trin, from Latin trīnus.

parole.significato: An object, usually in the form of a statuette, cup, or shield, awarded for success in a competition or to mark a specia…
parole.testo: From Middle French trophée, from Latin trophaeum (“a sign of victory, a monument”), tropaeum, from Ancient Greek τρόπαιον (trópaion, “monument of an enemy's defeat”), from neuter of τροπαῖος (tropaîos, “of defeat”), from τροπή (tropḗ, “a rout, a turning of an enemy”). Doublet of tropæum.

parole.significato: Cruel or savage.
parole.testo: First attested circa 1540, from Middle French, from Latin truculentus (“fierce, savage”), from trux (“fierce, wild”).

parole.significato: To supply with, or enclose in, a tube.
parole.testo: From Middle French tube, from Latin tubus (“tube, pipe”), related to tuba (“long trumpet; war-trumpet”), of obscure ultimate origin, but possibly connected to tībia (“shinbone, reed-pipe”); see there. Doublet of tubus.

parole.significato: To turn (a laminar flow) into a turbulent flow.
parole.testo: From turbul(ent) + -ate (verb-forming suffix), from Middle English turbulent, from Middle French turbulent, from Latin turbulentus, from turba (“disorder, tumult, crowd”).

parole.significato: Violently disturbed or agitated; tempestuous, tumultuous.
parole.testo: From Middle English turbulent, from Middle French turbulent, from Latin turbulentus, from turba (“disorder, tumult, crowd”).

parole.significato: Inherent baseness, depravity or wickedness; corruptness and evilness.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French turpitude, from Latin turpitūdō (“baseness, infamy”), from turpis (“foul, base”).

parole.significato: Fertile growth, abundance, fruitfulness; copiousness, plenty.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English uberte, from Middle French uberté, from Latin ūbertās, from ūber (“womb”).

parole.significato: Of a reddish brown colour, like that of the pigment.
parole.testo: From Middle French ombre (“umber”), from terre d'ombre (“dark ochre”), from Old French umbre (“shade, shadow”), from Latin umbra. Doublet of umbra.

parole.significato: A feeling of anger or annoyance caused by something offensive.
parole.testo: From Middle French ombrage (“umbrage”), from Old French ombrage, from Latin umbrāticus (“in the shade”), from umbra (“shadow, shade”).

parole.significato: Unvarying; all the same.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French uniforme, from Latin uniformis.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, characteristic of, or happening or located in, a city or town; of, pertaining to, or characteristic…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French urbain (“belonging to a city, urban; courteous, refined, urbane”) (modern French urbain), or from its etymon Latin urbānus (“of or belonging to a city, urban; of manners or style: like those of city dwellers: cultivated, polished, refined, sophisticated”) + English -an (s

parole.significato: Behaviour that is polished, refined, courteous.
parole.testo: From Middle English urbanitie, from Middle French urbanité, from Latin urbānitās, from urbānus (“belonging to a city”), with a sense of "having the manners of townspeople" in Classical Latin, from urbs (“city”); equivalent to urbane + -ity (sense 1) and urban + -ity (sense 2).

parole.significato: Synonym of aurochs.
parole.testo: From Middle French ure or its etymon Latin ūrus. Doublet of urus.

parole.significato: Requiring immediate attention.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French urgent (“pressing, impelling”), from Latin urgēns, from urgēre (“to press”), from Proto-Indo-European *werǵʰ- (“bind, squeeze”). Equivalent to urge + -ent. Related to German würgen (“to strangle”), Lithuanian ver̃žti (“to string, tighten, constrict”), Russian (poetic) отв

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the uterus.
parole.testo: From Middle French utérin, from Latin uterinus (“pertaining to the womb; born of the same mother”), from Latin uterus (“womb”). Related to English uterus. By surface analysis, uter- + -ine.

parole.significato: Useful.
parole.testo: From Middle French utile, from Old French utele, from Latin ūtilis.

parole.significato: Not clearly expressed; stated in indefinite terms.
parole.testo: From Middle French vague, from Latin vagus (“uncertain, vague”, literally “wandering, rambling, strolling”).

parole.significato: Well-grounded or justifiable, pertinent.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French valide (“healthy, sound, in good order”), from Latin validus, from valeō (“to be strong, to be healthy, to be worth”) + -idus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂welh₁- (“be strong”).

parole.significato: The act of varying; a partial change in the form, position, state, or qualities of a thing.
parole.testo: From Middle French variation, from Old French variacion, from Latin variātiō, from vary + -ation.

parole.significato: More than one (of an indeterminate set of things).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French varieux, from Latin varius (“manifold, diverse, various, parti-colored, variegated, also changing, changeable, fickle, etc.”). By surface analysis, vary + -ous.

parole.significato: An upright open container used mainly for displaying fresh, dried, or artificial flowers.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French vase, from Latin vās. Doublet of vas.

parole.significato: Very large or wide (literally or figuratively).
parole.testo: From Middle French vaste, from Latin vastus (“void, immense”). Related to waste and German Wüste.

parole.significato: Emptiness or desolation.
parole.testo: From vast + -ity, from Middle French vastité or its source, Latin vastitas. Compare Middle English wastite.

parole.significato: A vector quantity that denotes the rate of change of position with respect to time, combining speed with a directional…
parole.testo: From Middle French vélocité, from Latin vēlōcitās (“speed”), from vēlōx (“fast”), thus a doublet of veloce.

parole.significato: Commanding respect because of age, dignity, character or position.
parole.testo: From Middle French vénérable, from Old French, from Latin venerabilis.

parole.significato: The act of venerating or the state of being venerated.
parole.testo: From Middle French vénération, from Old French veneracion, from Latin veneratio.

parole.significato: The hunting of wild animals.
parole.testo: From Middle English venerie, borrowed from Middle French venerie, from Old French venerie (“hunting”), derived from vener, from Latin vēnor (“to hunt”).

parole.significato: An opening through which gases, especially air, can pass.
parole.testo: Partly from Middle French vent, from Latin ventus and partly from French éventer. Cognate with French vent and Spanish viento (“wind”) and ventana (“window”). Doublet of wind.

parole.significato: Having a big belly.
parole.testo: From Middle French ventripotent, from Latin venter (“belly”) + potens (“powerful”).

parole.significato: A rod or staff of office, e.g. of a verger.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French verge (“rod or wand of office”), hence "scope, territory dominated", from Latin virga (“shoot, rod stick”), of unknown origin. parole.significato: The property of seeming true, of resembling reality; resemblance to reality.
parole.testo: From Middle French vérisimilitude, from Latin vērīsimilitūdō (“likeness to truth”), more correctly written separately as vērī similitūdō; from vērī, genitive singular of vērus (“true, real”), + similitūdō (“likeness, resemblance”).

parole.significato: True; genuine.
parole.testo: From verity + -able, from Middle French veritable, from Old French veritable, from Latin veritabilis.

parole.significato: Having an aspect of great depth, drawing the eye to look downwards.
parole.testo: From Middle French vertigineux, from Latin vertīginōsus.

parole.significato: A membrane-bound compartment found in a cell.
parole.testo: From Middle French vesicule, from Latin vēsīcula. By surface analysis, vesic- + -le. Doublet of vesicule.

parole.significato: A person with long experience of a particular activity.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French vétéran, from Latin veterānus.

parole.significato: Regular change or succession from one thing to another, or one part of a cycle to the next; alternation; mutual success…
parole.testo: From Middle French vicissitude, from Latin vicissitūdō (“change”), from vicissim (“on the other hand, in turn”), from vicis (“change, vicissitude”), whence Portuguese vez and French fois (“time (as in "next time"), occurrence”).

parole.significato: One that is harmed—killed, injured, subjected to oppression, deceit, or otherwise adversely affected—by someone or some…
parole.testo: From Middle French victime, from Latin victima (“sacrificial animal”). Although this root and victor drive from homophonous PIE roots, they are traditionally reconstructed as separate words and thus not cognates.

parole.significato: A person whose role it is to kill the sacrificial victim(s) during a ritual sacrifice.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French victimaire, from Latin victimārius, from victima + -ārius.

parole.significato: One of a class of temporal officers who originally represented the bishops, but later were given status of fiefs, and b…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French vidame, from Latin vice-dominus, from Latin vice (“instead of”) + dominus (“master, lord”).

parole.significato: Alert watchfulness.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French vigilance, from Latin vigilantia.

parole.significato: The act or an instance of violating or the condition of being violated.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French violation, from Latin violātiō (“injury, profanation”), from violō (“to treat with violence; to maltreat; to violate, defile, profane”). Morphologically violate + -ion.

parole.significato: A venomous snake in the family Viperidae.
parole.testo: From Middle French vipere, from Old French vipre, from Latin vīpera, contracted from vīvipara f (“viviparous”, adj.), from vīvus (“alive”, adj.) + parere (“to bear”, verb). Doublet of weever and wyvern.

parole.significato: Being or resembling a virgin.
parole.testo: From Middle English virginal, from Middle French virginal, from Latin virginālis. The musical instrument is probably so called from being played by young girls.

parole.significato: A medieval punctuation mark similar to the slash ⟨/⟩ or pipe ⟨|⟩ and used as a scratch comma and caesura mark.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French virgule, from Latin virgula (“twig; scratch comma”), from virga (“rod, branch”) + -ulus (diminutive suffix). Doublet of virgula.

parole.significato: Manly; having characteristics associated with being male, such as strength; exhibiting masculine traits to an exaggerat…
parole.testo: From Middle French viril, from Latin virīlis, from vir (“man”, “male human”) + -īlis (suffix forming adjectives from nouns).

parole.significato: The state of being virile.
parole.testo: From virile + -ity, from Middle French virilité, from Latin virīlitās.

parole.significato: The capacity to live and develop.
parole.testo: From vital + -ity, from Middle French vitalité, from Latin vitalitas (“vital force, life”), from vitalis (“vital”); see vital.

parole.significato: vitreous humour
parole.testo: From vitreous, from Middle French vitreux, from Latin vitreus (“glassy, transparent”), from vitrum (“glass”).

parole.significato: Of or resembling glass; glassy.
parole.testo: From Middle French vitreux, from Latin vitreus (“glassy, transparent”), from vitrum (“glass”). parole.significato: To convert into glass or a glass-like substance by heat and fusion.
parole.testo: From Middle French vitrifier, from Latin vitrum (“glass”).

parole.significato: A word or utterance, especially with reference to its form rather than its meaning.
parole.testo: From Middle English vocable, from Middle French vocable and its etymon, Latin vocābulum, from vocō (“to call”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to calling; used in calling or vocation.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English [Term?], borrowed from Middle French vocatif, from Latin vocātīvus (“for calling”); a calque of Ancient Greek κλητῐκή (klētĭkḗ, “for calling; vocative case”) – from vocāre (“to call”), from Proto-Indo-European *wokʷ-, o-grade of *wekʷ- (“give vocal utterance, speak”). See La

parole.significato: Having extended wings as if flying.
parole.testo: From Middle French volant, present participle of voler (“to fly”), from Latin volāre.

parole.significato: Evaporating or vaporizing readily under normal conditions.
parole.testo: From Middle French volatile, from Latin volātilis (“flying; swift; temporary; volatile”), from volō (“to fly”).

parole.significato: Turning or whirling; winding.
parole.testo: From Middle French volubile, from Latin volūbilis (“rolling”), from volvō (“to roll”). Doublet of voluble.

parole.significato: Fluent or having a ready flow of speech.
parole.testo: From Middle French volubile, from Latin volūbilis (“rolling”), from volvō (“roll”).

parole.significato: Characterized or marked by full, generous, pleasurable sensation.
parole.testo: From Middle French voluptueux, from Latin voluptuōsus (“delightful”), from voluptās (“pleasure, delight”), from volup (“with pleasure”).

parole.significato: The state of being voracious; rapacity or extreme gluttony.
parole.testo: First attested in 1526 from Middle French voracité, from Latin vorācitās (whence -acity), from vorāx.

parole.significato: Dedicated or given in fulfillment of a vow or pledge.
parole.testo: From Middle French votif, from Latin vōtīvus (“votive”), from vōtum (“vow”).
